sk: आविः संनिहितं गुहाचरं नाम महत्पदमत्रैतत्समर्पितम् एजत्प्राणन्निमिषच्च यदेतज्जानत सदसद्वरेण्यं परं विज्ञानाद्यद्वरिष्ठं प्रजानाम् ||
ro: āviḥ · saṁnihitaṁ · guhā-caraṁ · nāma · mahat · padam · atra · etat · samarpitam · ejat · prāṇat · nimiṣat · ca · yat · etat · jānata · sat · asat · vareṇyaṁ · paraṁ · vijñānāt · yat · variṣṭhaṁ · prajānām ||
hi: जो आविः (manifest / प्रकट) है और संनिहित (close at hand / अति निकट) है, गुहाचर (moving in the cave [of the heart] / हृदय-गुहा में विचरने वाला) — वह महत् पद (great abode / महान् पद) है — यहीं (अत्र) यह सब समर्पित (centered / placed) है। जो यह एजत् (moving / गतिशील), प्राणत् (breathing / प्राणयुक्त), निमिषत् (blinking / पलक झपकने वाला) [जगत् है] — जानो इसे सत् और असत् [दोनों से] वरेण्य (most worthy of choice / सर्वश्रेष्ठ) — प्रजाओं (beings) के विज्ञान (understanding) से भी परं वरिष्ठ (supremely excellent / सर्वोत्कृष्ट)।
en: That which is manifest (āviḥ) and close at hand (saṁnihitam), moving in the cave [of the heart] (guhā-caram) — that is the great abode (mahat padam); in it all this is centered (samarpitam). That which moves (ejat), breathes (prāṇat), and blinks (nimiṣat) — know it as both being and non-being (sat-asat), the most worthy of choice (vareṇyam), supreme (param), beyond [all] understanding (vijñānāt), the most excellent (variṣṭham) of beings (prajānām).

ws.e: manifest / evident — that which is openly present; Brahman is not hidden in some remote heaven but is manifest, right here; paradoxically combined with guhā-cara (moving in the cave)

ws.h: अति निकट / समीप / close at hand
ws.e: close at hand / present nearby — sam + ni + √dhā (placed near); Brahman is not far away but intimately present; closer than close
moving in the cave — guhā (cave) + cara (moving); the Self 'moves' in the cave of the heart; cf. Kaṭha 1.2.12 — guhāhitam; it is both 'hidden' and 'moving' — not static but alive
moving — from √ej (to stir/move); the living, dynamic universe; cf. Īśā 1.4: 'tad ejati tan naijati' — it moves, it moves not

ws.h: वरण करने योग्य / सर्वश्रेष्ठ / most worthy of choice
ws.e: most worthy of choice — from √vṛ (to choose); the same word used in the Gāyatrī mantra (tat savituḥ vareṇyam); Brahman is the supreme object of choice/desire
most excellent — superlative of vara (excellent); the highest of all beings; nothing surpasses it

gr: The paradox of Brahman: this opening mantra of Khanda 2 introduces Brahman through paradox — it is simultaneously āviḥ (manifest, openly present) AND guhā-caram (hidden in the cave of the heart). It is close at hand (saṁnihitam) yet beyond all understanding (vijñānāt param). mahat padam — 'the great abode': Brahman is the place (padam) where everything rests. All that moves, breathes, and blinks is 'centered' (samarpitam) in it. ejat prāṇat nimiṣat — 'moving, breathing, blinking': these three verbs capture the entire living world — locomotion (ejat), respiration (prāṇat), and the blink reflex (nimiṣat). Everything that is alive, in any way, is an expression of Brahman. vareṇyam: this word connects to the Gāyatrī mantra (ṚV 3.62.10) — 'tat savitur vareṇyam bhargo devasya dhīmahi' — establishing Brahman as the supreme object of contemplation.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_2.2.1 — The paradox of āviḥ (manifest) + guhā-caram (hidden in the cave) echoes the Īśā Upanishad's paradoxes (1.4-5: 'it moves, it moves not; it is far, it is near'). The word 'vareṇyam' connects this mantra to the Gāyatrī mantra — the most sacred verse in the Vedas — suggesting that what the Gāyatrī points to (the light of Savitṛ) is the same Brahman the Muṇḍaka teaches. The phrase 'vijñānāt param' (beyond understanding) echoes the Kaṭha (1.3.10-11) hierarchy: objects → senses → mind → buddhi → mahān ātmā → avyakta → puruṣa. Brahman is 'beyond' all cognitive faculties, not because it is unknowable but because it is the knower — the subject cannot objectify itself.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'आविः' = ब्रह्म प्रकट (manifest) है — क्योंकि ब्रह्म = आत्मा = सबको प्रत्यक्ष — 'अहम् अस्मि' (I am) यह अनुभव ही ब्रह्म है। 'गुहाचरम्' = फिर भी गुहा (हृदय) में छिपा — क्योंकि अज्ञान (avidyā) ने ढँक रखा है। 'विज्ञानात् परम्' = बुद्धि से परे — क्योंकि ब्रह्म विषय (object) नहीं — ज्ञाता (knower) ही है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'āviḥ' = Brahman is manifest — because Brahman = ātman = directly known to everyone — the experience 'I am' IS Brahman. 'Guhā-caram' = yet hidden in the cave (heart) — because avidyā (ignorance) covers it. 'Vijñānāt param' = beyond the intellect — because Brahman is not an object but the knower itself.
advaita.ins: Brahman is the most obvious thing in the universe — it's your own 'I am.' You've never been without it for a single moment. Yet it's also the most hidden — because you're always looking outward for what is already inside. The eye cannot see itself. The knower cannot know itself as an object.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'आविः संनिहितम्' = भगवान् प्रकट और समीप — शास्त्र (scripture) और अनुग्रह (grace) के द्वारा। 'गुहाचरम्' = भगवान् प्रत्येक जीव के हृदय में अन्तर्यामी (inner controller) रूप में विराजमान। 'वरेण्यम्' = भगवान् ही एकमात्र प्राप्य (goal) और वरणीय (worthy of choice) हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'āviḥ saṁnihitam' = the Lord is manifest and near — through scripture and grace. 'Guhā-caram' = the Lord dwells in every being's heart as antaryāmī (inner controller). 'Vareṇyam' = the Lord alone is the ultimate goal and worthy of choice.
vishisht.ins: God is not hiding from you — He's standing right next to you, manifest and near. He's also inside you, moving in the cave of your heart. The most evident and the most intimate — at the same time. And He is the one thing truly worth choosing.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'आविः' = चेतना प्रकट — सब कुछ में विद्यमान — प्रत्येक गतिशील (ejat), प्राणवान् (prāṇat), निमिषित (nimiṣat) वस्तु में। 'गुहाचरम्' = वही चेतना हृदय-गुहा में — अन्तर्मुखी (inward-turned)। 'महत् पदम्' = चेतना का महान् स्थान — जहाँ सब केन्द्रित (centered) है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'āviḥ' = consciousness is manifest — present in everything — in every moving, breathing, blinking thing. 'Guhā-caram' = the same consciousness moves inward in the cave of the heart. 'Mahat padam' = the great station of consciousness — where all is centered.
aurobindo.ins: Look around: everything moves, breathes, blinks. That's consciousness, manifest. Now look inward: the same consciousness moves in the cave of your heart. Outside and inside, it's the same presence — manifest everywhere, intimate here. The great abode is both the cosmos and your own chest.

dp.q: 🔍 The paradox: manifest yet hidden
dp.a: The opening of Mundaka 2.2 presents one of the Upanishads' most characteristic paradoxes — Brahman is simultaneously āviḥ (manifest, openly evident) AND guhā-caram (hidden in the cave of the heart): How is Brahman 'manifest'? Because Brahman = consciousness = the 'I am' that everyone experiences. You have never been without consciousness for a single instant. It is the most self-evident fact of existence — more evident than any object, because objects are known through consciousness, while consciousness is self-known. As Shankara says: 'ātmā is pratyakṣa (directly evident) to everyone.' How is Brahman 'hidden'? Because although consciousness is always present, we habitually look through it at objects rather than at it. The eye sees everything but cannot see itself. Similarly, consciousness illuminates everything but is itself overlooked — hidden in plain sight, 'moving in the cave' of the heart. The Īśā parallel (mantra 5): 'tad ejati tan naijati, tad dūre tad vad antike' — 'It moves, It moves not; It is far, It is near.' The same paradox: Brahman is simultaneously distant (transcendent) and near (immanent), moving and still. The resolution: the paradox is not a logical contradiction but a description of two perspectives. From the standpoint of ordinary consciousness, Brahman is hidden — we are ignorant of our own nature. From the standpoint of realisation, Brahman is manifest — there was never a moment when it was absent.

dp.q: 🔍 'Vareṇyam' — the connection to the Gāyatrī mantra
dp.a: The word 'vareṇyam' (most worthy of choice) creates a powerful link to the Gāyatrī mantra, the most sacred verse in the Vedas: The Gāyatrī (ṚV 3.62.10): 'oṁ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ / tat savitur vareṇyaṁ / bhargo devasya dhīmahi / dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt' — 'We meditate upon the most worthy of choice (vareṇyam) radiance (bharga) of the divine Savitṛ (the Sun); may He inspire our intellects.' The connection: by using 'vareṇyam' to describe Brahman, the Muṇḍaka is saying that what the Gāyatrī mantra points to — the supreme light (bharga) of Savitṛ — is the same Brahman taught here. The Gāyatrī's 'vareṇyam bharga' and the Muṇḍaka's 'vareṇyam param' are the same reality. Why 'worthy of choice'? Brahman is not something imposed upon you. It is something you choose — the highest object of desire, the supreme goal. The word 'vareṇyam' implies that knowing Brahman is an act of the will as much as the intellect — you must turn toward it, choose it above all other pursuits. The implication for sādhana: every recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra is an implicit meditation on Brahman. The millions who chant the Gāyatrī daily are already contemplating 'vareṇyam' — the supreme reality — whether they know it or not.

sk: यदर्चिमद्यदणुभ्योऽणु च यस्मिँल्लोका निहिता लोकिनश्च तदेतदक्षरं ब्रह्म स प्राणस्तदु वाङ्मनः तदेतत्सत्यं तदमृतं तद्वेद्धव्यं सोम्य विद्धि ||
ro: yat · arcimat · yat · aṇubhyaḥ · aṇu · ca · yasmin · lokāḥ · nihitāḥ · lokinaḥ · ca · tat · etat · akṣaraṁ · brahma · saḥ · prāṇaḥ · tat · u · vāk · manaḥ · tat · etat · satyaṁ · tat · amṛtaṁ · tat · veddhavyaṁ · somya · viddhi ||
hi: जो अर्चिमत् (luminous / ज्योतिर्मय) है, जो अणु से भी अणु (subtler than the subtle / सूक्ष्म से भी सूक्ष्म) है, जिसमें लोक (worlds) और लोकिनः (inhabitants of worlds / लोकवासी) निहित (placed / स्थापित) हैं — वह यह अक्षर ब्रह्म (Imperishable Brahman) है। वह प्राण (life-breath) है; वही वाक् (speech) और मनस् (mind) है। वह सत्य (truth) है, वह अमृत (immortal) है, वह वेद्धव्य (to be pierced / भेदने / जानने योग्य) है — हे सोम्य (gentle one)! विद्धि (know it / जानो)!
en: That which is luminous (arcimat), that which is subtler than the subtle (aṇubhyo'ṇu), in which the worlds (lokāḥ) and their inhabitants (lokinaḥ) are placed (nihitāḥ) — that is this Imperishable Brahman (akṣaram brahma). It is prāṇa (life-breath); it is speech (vāk) and mind (manas). It is truth (satya), it is immortal (amṛta), it is to be pierced (veddhavyam) — O gentle one (somya), know it (viddhi)!

ws.e: luminous / radiant — arci (flame/ray) + mat (possessing); Brahman possesses its own radiance; self-luminous (svayam-prakāśa)
subtler than the subtle — aṇu (atom/minute) in double comparative; Brahman is smaller than the smallest conceivable thing; cf. Kaṭha 1.2.20 and Śvetāśvatara 3.20
inhabitants of the worlds — loka (world) + in (possessing/dwelling in); all beings who dwell in the worlds; the worlds AND their contents rest in Brahman

ws.h: भेदने योग्य / जानने योग्य / to be pierced
ws.e: to be pierced / to be hit (as a target) — from √vyadh (to pierce); the same root as in archery; anticipates the bow-and-arrow metaphor of the next mantra; Brahman is the target to be 'pierced' by the arrow of meditation
know! — imperative of √vid (to know); a direct command from teacher to student; also puns on √vyadh (to pierce) — 'know' and 'pierce' converge

gr: Brahman described and commanded: this mantra serves as both a description and a command — it describes Brahman (luminous, subtler than subtle, containing all worlds) and commands the student to 'know' / 'pierce' it. arcimat + aṇubhyo'ṇu: the paradox of size — Brahman is luminous (vast, radiant) AND subtler than the subtle (smaller than the smallest). The Kaṭha (1.2.20) uses exactly this paradox: 'aṇor aṇīyān mahato mahīyān' — 'smaller than the small, greater than the great.' veddhavyam — 'to be pierced': this is a deliberate setup for the bow-and-arrow metaphor in the next mantra (2.2.3-4). The word comes from √vyadh (to pierce/hit a target) — the same root used in archery. Brahman is the target; the student must aim at it and 'pierce' it with concentrated meditation. viddhi — 'know!': the imperative is urgent. The teacher is not suggesting but commanding. And the word 'viddhi' puns on 'veddhavyam' — 'know it' and 'pierce it' share a resonance, suggesting that true knowledge IS a piercing — a direct penetration.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_2.2.2 — The word 'veddhavyam' (to be pierced) directly anticipates the bow-and-arrow meditation of 2.2.3-4 — it establishes Brahman as a 'target' (lakṣya) to be hit. The paradox 'arcimat + aṇubhyo'ṇu' (luminous + subtler than subtle) is one of the Upanishads' most characteristic descriptions — cf. Kaṭha 1.2.20 ('aṇor aṇīyān mahato mahīyān'), Śvetāśvatara 3.20 ('aṇor aṇīyān mahato mahīyān ātmā guhāyāṁ nihito'sya jantoḥ'). The equation 'saḥ prāṇaḥ, tad u vāk manaḥ' connects Brahman to the three fundamental functions — life (prāṇa), expression (vāk), and cognition (manas) — all three are Brahman. The imperative 'viddhi' (know!) is rare in the Upanishads and conveys urgency.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'अणुभ्योऽणु' = ब्रह्म सूक्ष्मतम — किसी भी इन्द्रिय या मन से ग्राह्य नहीं। 'अर्चिमत्' = फिर भी स्वयंप्रकाश (self-luminous) — अपने प्रकाश से सब कुछ प्रकाशित करता है। 'वेद्धव्यम्' = भेदने योग्य — ध्यान (meditation) के तीक्ष्ण बाण (sharp arrow) से — अगला मन्त्र इसी को विस्तार देगा।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'aṇubhyo'ṇu' = Brahman is the subtlest — not graspable by any sense or mind. 'Arcimat' = yet self-luminous — it illuminates everything by its own light. 'Veddhavyam' = to be pierced — by the sharp arrow of meditation — the next mantra will elaborate this.
advaita.ins: Brahman is subtler than an atom — you can't catch it with your senses. But it's also luminous — it lights up everything you see. How do you find something that's everywhere yet beyond all perception? You pierce it — with the arrow of focused meditation. The next mantra tells you how.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'अक्षरं ब्रह्म' = परमात्मा — जिसमें सब लोक और लोकवासी निहित। 'सः प्राणः, तदु वाक् मनः' = भगवान् ही सब का प्राण, वाणी, और मन — भगवान् बिना कुछ भी जीवित/अभिव्यक्त/चेतन नहीं। 'विद्धि' = जानो — भक्ति (devotion) और ध्यान (meditation) से।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'akṣaram brahma' = the Supreme Lord — in whom all worlds and inhabitants rest. 'Saḥ prāṇaḥ, tad u vāk manaḥ' = the Lord is the prāṇa, speech, and mind of all — nothing lives, speaks, or thinks without the Lord. 'Viddhi' = know — through devotion and meditation.
vishisht.ins: The Lord is the life in your breath, the meaning in your words, the awareness in your mind. Without Him, breath is just air, words are just noise, mind is just chemistry. He gives everything its reality. Know Him — and know the source of everything you are.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'अर्चिमत्' = चेतना = स्वयं-प्रकाशमान (self-luminous consciousness)। 'अणुभ्योऽणु' = चेतना = सूक्ष्मतम — पदार्थ (matter) के भीतर भी। 'वेद्धव्यम्' = चेतना को 'भेदना' = चेतना में सीधे प्रवेश — बौद्धिक (intellectual) नहीं, अनुभवात्मक (experiential)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'arcimat' = consciousness = self-luminous. 'Aṇubhyo'ṇu' = consciousness is the subtlest — present even within matter. 'Veddhavyam' = to 'pierce' consciousness = direct entry into consciousness — not intellectual but experiential.
aurobindo.ins: Consciousness is luminous — it shines by itself. It's subtler than an atom — it's inside the atom. It IS the atom's interiority. You can't think your way to it — you have to pierce through the layers of thought and enter it directly. That's what the next mantra's archery metaphor teaches.

dp.q: 🔍 'Veddhavyam' — Brahman as target to be pierced
dp.a: The word 'veddhavyam' (to be pierced) is a deliberate and crucial setup for the famous bow-and-arrow meditation that follows in mantras 3-4: Etymology: veddhavya = the gerundive of √vyadh (to pierce/hit). It is an archery term — 'that which is to be pierced,' i.e., the target. The metaphor anticipated: Brahman is the target. The student is the archer. The arrow is the ātman (self). The bow is the syllable OM. The act of 'knowing' Brahman is reframed as an act of hitting a target — not passive reception of information but an active, concentrated, one-pointed aim. The pun: 'veddhavyam' (to be pierced, from √vyadh) puns with 'viddhi' (know!, from √vid). In Sanskrit, 'knowing' and 'piercing' share a phonetic resonance — suggesting that true knowledge is not a gentle understanding but a penetration, a direct entry into the heart of reality. The practical implication: meditation is not vague contemplation — it is targeted, concentrated, arrow-like. The mind must be as focused as an archer's eye on the bullseye. Distraction is missing the target. Concentration is hitting it.

dp.q: 🔍 'Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great'
dp.a: The phrase 'aṇubhyo'ṇu' (subtler than the subtle) is one of the Upanishads' most famous descriptions of Brahman, usually paired with its opposite — 'mahato mahīyān' (greater than the great): The Kaṭha's full version (1.2.20): 'aṇor aṇīyān mahato mahīyān ātmāsya jantor nihito guhāyām' — 'Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great, the Self is hidden in the cave of this being.' The Śvetāśvatara's version (3.20): nearly identical — 'aṇor aṇīyān mahato mahīyān ātmā guhāyāṁ nihito'sya jantoḥ.' What this paradox means: (1) Subtler than the subtle: Brahman is not a 'thing' — it cannot be detected by any instrument, perceived by any sense, or conceived by any thought. It is subtler than atoms, subtler than space, subtler than consciousness itself (since it is the ground of consciousness). (2) Greater than the great: Brahman is not merely small/subtle — it also contains all worlds, all beings, all space. The entire universe rests IN it. (3) The paradox is the point: Brahman cannot be captured by either extreme. It is not big, not small, not both, not neither. It transcends all categories of size. The paradox is a deliberate tool to break the mind's categories and force a shift to non-conceptual awareness.

sk: धनुर्गृहीत्वौपनिषदं महास्त्रं शरं ह्युपासानिशितं सन्धयीत आयम्य तद्भावगतेन चेतसा लक्ष्यं तदेवाक्षरं सोम्य विद्धि ||
ro: dhanuḥ · gṛhītvā · aupaniṣadaṁ · mahā-astraṁ · śaraṁ · hi · upāsā-niśitaṁ · sandhayīta · āyamya · tat-bhāva-gatena · cetasā · lakṣyaṁ · tat · eva · akṣaraṁ · somya · viddhi ||
hi: उपनिषद् (Upanishadic) महा-अस्त्र (great weapon) — धनुः (bow) को — गृहीत्वा (taking up / उठाकर); उपासना से निशित (शान पर चढ़ाया / sharpened by meditation) शर (arrow) को सन्धयीत (fix on the bowstring / चढ़ाओ); तद्-भाव-गतेन चेतसा (with mind absorbed in That / उस [ब्रह्म] के भाव में लीन चित्त से) आयम्य (drawing [the bow] / खींचकर) — हे सोम्य (gentle one)! लक्ष्य (the target) वह अक्षर (Imperishable) ही है — विद्धि (pierce it / भेदो)!
en: Taking up (gṛhītvā) the great weapon (mahā-astra) of the Upanishad — the bow (dhanus) — fix (sandhayīta) upon it the arrow (śara) sharpened (niśita) by meditation (upāsā); then, drawing [the bow] (āyamya) with the mind absorbed in That (tat-bhāva-gatena cetasā) — the target (lakṣya) is the Imperishable (akṣara) itself, O gentle one (somya) — pierce it (viddhi)!

ws.e: bow — the instrument of the archer; here = the Upanishadic teaching / the syllable OM (identified in the next mantra); the bow provides the framework and the tension
pertaining to the Upanishad — the bow is 'Upanishadic' = it comes from the secret teaching; the Upanishad itself is the weapon
great weapon — mahā (great) + astra (weapon/missile); the Upanishadic teaching is not just knowledge but a weapon — it destroys ignorance
sharpened by meditation — upāsā (worship/meditation) + niśita (whetted/sharpened); the arrow is not effective unless sharpened — meditation sharpens the mind into a point

ws.h: उसके (ब्रह्म के) भाव में गत (absorbed) चित्त से
ws.e: with mind gone into the state/being of That — tat (That/Brahman) + bhāva (state/being) + gata (gone into) + cetasā (with consciousness); the mind must be completely absorbed in Brahman
target — from √lakṣ (to mark/aim at); Brahman is the target; the same word used for an archer's bullseye

gr: The bow-and-arrow meditation: this is the Muṇḍaka's most famous and most practical teaching — the archery metaphor for meditation on Brahman. The components: (1) Bow (dhanus) = the Upanishadic teaching — specifically, the syllable OM (as the next mantra makes explicit). (2) Arrow (śara) = the individual self (ātman) — the meditator's own consciousness, sharpened by upāsanā (meditation). (3) Target (lakṣya) = Brahman / the akṣara (Imperishable). (4) Drawing the bow (āyamya) = the concentration of mind — pulling the consciousness taut with total absorption (tat-bhāva-gatena cetasā). (5) Piercing (viddhi) = realisation — the moment of direct contact between the individual self and Brahman. upāsā-niśitam — 'sharpened by meditation': the arrow must be sharpened. An unsharpened arrow (an unprepared mind) will bounce off the target. Meditation is the whetstone that makes the mind pointed enough to pierce through to Brahman. tat-bhāva-gatena cetasā — 'with mind absorbed in That': the archer must be completely focused. Not half-focused, not distracted — the mind must have 'gone into the state of That' (tat-bhāva-gata). Total absorption. mahā-astra — 'great weapon': the Upanishadic teaching is called a 'weapon' — it destroys ignorance, not by argument but by direct realisation.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_2.2.3 — The bow-and-arrow meditation (dhanuḥ-śara-upāsanā) is one of the most iconic images in the Upanishads and has deeply influenced later traditions. The archery metaphor appears in no other Upanishad in this precise form, making it uniquely Muṇḍaka. However, the Chāndogya (1.3.5) and Kaṭha (1.2.12) use the language of 'piercing' and 'target' in related contexts. The term 'mahā-astra' (great weapon) is striking — the Upanishad is literally called a 'weapon,' implying that jñāna (knowledge) is not merely contemplative but actively destructive of avidyā (ignorance). The compound 'tat-bhāva-gatena cetasā' describes what later Yoga philosophy calls samādhi — complete absorption of mind in the object of meditation.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — धनुष = ओंकार (OM); शर = जीवात्मा (individual self); लक्ष्य = ब्रह्म। शर 'उपासना से तीक्ष्ण' = चित्त-शुद्धि (purification of mind)। 'तद्भावगतेन चेतसा' = निदिध्यासन (deep meditation) — चित्त ब्रह्म-भाव में लीन। 'विद्धि' = लक्ष्य भेदो = ब्रह्म-साक्षात्कार (direct realisation)।
advaita.en: Shankara says bow = OM; arrow = the individual self (jīvātman); target = Brahman. Arrow 'sharpened by meditation' = purification of mind. 'Tat-bhāva-gatena cetasā' = nididhyāsana (deep meditation) — mind absorbed in Brahman. 'Viddhi' = pierce the target = direct realisation of Brahman.
advaita.ins: Take up OM as your bow. Place yourself — your very self — as the arrow. Sharpen yourself with meditation until your mind is a single point. Draw the bow with total concentration. And let go. When the arrow hits, you and the target are one. That's realisation.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — धनुष = उपनिषद् शिक्षा (Upanishadic teaching); शर = भक्ति-पूत आत्मा (devotion-purified soul); लक्ष्य = भगवान्। 'उपासानिशितम्' = भक्ति (devotion) और ध्यान (meditation) से तीक्ष्ण। 'तद्भावगतेन चेतसा' = भगवान् में एकाग्र (one-pointed in God)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says bow = Upanishadic teaching; arrow = the devotion-purified soul; target = the Lord. 'Upāsā-niśitam' = sharpened by devotion and meditation. 'Tat-bhāva-gatena cetasā' = one-pointed in God.
vishisht.ins: The Upanishad is your bow — it provides the framework, the power. Your soul is the arrow — purified by devotion, sharpened by meditation. And God is the target — the only thing worth aiming at. Draw the bow with love, release with surrender. When the arrow reaches God, you've come home.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — धनुष = चेतना की एकाग्रता का साधन (instrument of concentration); शर = व्यक्तिगत चेतना (individual consciousness); लक्ष्य = विश्व-चेतना / सच्चिदानन्द। 'उपासानिशितम्' = योग-अभ्यास (yoga practice) से तीक्ष्ण। 'विद्धि' = चेतना-रूपान्तर (transformation of consciousness)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says bow = the instrument of concentration; arrow = individual consciousness; target = universal consciousness / Sat-Chit-Ānanda. 'Upāsā-niśitam' = sharpened by yoga practice. 'Viddhi' = transformation of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: Your consciousness is the arrow. Sharpen it with yoga — make it one-pointed, concentrated, undistracted. The bow is the method; the target is the Infinite. When the arrow of your focused consciousness hits the target, it doesn't bounce back — it merges. You don't just know the Infinite; you become it.

dp.q: 🔍 The bow-and-arrow meditation — the Muṇḍaka's most famous image
dp.a: The bow-and-arrow meditation (dhanuḥ-śara-upāsanā) is the Muṇḍaka's most celebrated and most practically applicable teaching: The complete mapping (combining mantras 3 and 4): (1) Bow (dhanus) = the syllable OM (praṇava) — as the next mantra makes explicit. The bow is the instrument — the framework, the vehicle, the means. OM provides the tension, the power, the structure. (2) Arrow (śara) = the individual self (ātman) — the meditator's own consciousness, sharpened by upāsanā (meditation/devotion). The arrow must be sharp — an unprepared mind cannot pierce Brahman. (3) Target (lakṣya) = Brahman / the akṣara (Imperishable). The target is definite, specific — not a vague 'spiritual experience' but Brahman itself. (4) Drawing the bow (āyamya) = concentrating the mind — pulling consciousness taut until it is fully absorbed in Brahman (tat-bhāva-gata). (5) Releasing / Piercing (viddhi) = the moment of realisation — when the arrow of the self hits the target of Brahman, and the two become one. Why archery? Archery requires: (a) Equipment — the right bow and arrow (preparation through study and practice). (b) Skill — sharpened by practice (upāsanā). (c) One-pointedness — the archer's eye is fixed on the target and nothing else. (d) Release — at the moment of release, there is no more effort; the arrow flies by its own momentum. Similarly, meditation requires preparation, practice, concentration, and ultimately a 'letting go' into realisation.

dp.q: 🔍 The Upanishad as 'great weapon' (mahā-astra)
dp.a: The Muṇḍaka calls the Upanishadic teaching a 'mahā-astra' (great weapon): What does this mean? The Upanishad is not merely a philosophical text or a source of spiritual inspiration — it is a weapon (astra). A weapon is designed to destroy. What does the Upanishadic weapon destroy? Avidyā (ignorance) — the root cause of saṁsāra (bondage). The warrior metaphor: the spiritual seeker is reframed as a warrior. The battlefield is the mind. The enemy is ignorance. The weapon is the Upanishad. The victory is liberation. This is not passive learning but active combat — you take up the bow, sharpen the arrow, draw with full strength, and fire. Comparison with the Bhagavad Gītā: the Gītā famously takes place on a battlefield, with Arjuna as warrior. The Muṇḍaka's archery metaphor anticipates this — the spiritual life is a battle, and knowledge is the supreme weapon. The Kaṭha's parallel (1.3.3-9): the Kaṭha uses the chariot metaphor — the Self is the rider, the body is the chariot, the intellect is the driver, the mind is the reins, the senses are the horses. Both metaphors (chariot and archery) describe the spiritual life in terms of focused, disciplined action — not passive contemplation but active engagement.

sk: प्रणवो धनुः शरोऽह्यात्मा ब्रह्म तल्लक्ष्यमुच्यते अप्रमत्तेन वेद्धव्यं शरवत्तन्मयो भवेत् ||
ro: praṇavaḥ · dhanuḥ · śaraḥ · hi · ātmā · brahma · tat · lakṣyam · ucyate · apramattena · veddhavyaṁ · śaravat · tat-mayaḥ · bhavet ||
hi: प्रणव (OM) धनुष (bow) है; आत्मा (the Self) ही शर (arrow) है; ब्रह्म ही वह लक्ष्य (target) कहा जाता (उच्यते) है। अप्रमत्तेन (with unwavering attention / बिना प्रमाद के) वेद्धव्यम् (it is to be pierced / भेदना है) — शर-वत् (like the arrow) तन्मय (one with That / तल्लीन) भवेत् (one should become / हो जाए)।
en: OM (praṇava) is the bow (dhanus); the Self (ātmā) is the arrow (śara); Brahman is said to be (ucyate) the target (lakṣya). It is to be pierced (veddhavyam) with unwavering attention (apramattena) — [and] like the arrow (śaravat), one should become one with That (tanmayo bhavet).

ws.e: the praṇava = OM — pra + √ṇu (to sound/praise); the sacred syllable; the essence of all the Vedas; the 'bow' that propels the arrow of the self toward Brahman
arrow — the Self (ātman) is the arrow; the meditator's own consciousness, aimed at Brahman
with unwavering attention — a (without) + pramatta (negligent/careless); the archer must be completely attentive; no distraction, no drowsiness, no wandering

ws.h: तत् (That/Brahman) में तल्लीन / absorbed in That
ws.e: made of That / one with That — tat (That) + maya (made of/consisting of); the arrow becomes one with the target; the self merges into Brahman

ws.h: शर (arrow) के समान / like an arrow
ws.e: like the arrow — just as an arrow, once it hits the target, remains embedded in it and becomes 'one' with it, the Self, once it reaches Brahman, merges and becomes one with Brahman

gr: The complete archery meditation: this mantra explicitly identifies each element: OM = bow, ātmā = arrow, Brahman = target. praṇavaḥ dhanuḥ — 'OM is the bow': OM is the vehicle, the launching mechanism. By meditating on OM, the consciousness is 'launched' toward Brahman. OM is not the goal but the means — it propels the arrow. śaro hy ātmā — 'the Self is the arrow': the meditator is not separate from the instrument of meditation. YOU are the arrow. It is not your thought that reaches Brahman — it is YOU. The whole self is launched. brahma tal lakṣyam — 'Brahman is the target': the target is definite and specific — Brahman, not 'relaxation,' not 'peace,' not 'spiritual experience,' but Brahman itself. apramattena veddhavyam — 'to be pierced with unwavering attention': apramāda (non-negligence) is critical. The archer who loses focus misses the target. The meditator who is careless (pramatta) will not reach Brahman. śaravat tanmayo bhavet — 'like the arrow, one should become one with That': this is the climax — the arrow, upon hitting the target, remains embedded in it. It does not bounce back. Similarly, the Self, upon reaching Brahman, becomes Brahman — tanmayaḥ (made of That). The meditator becomes what is meditated upon.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_2.2.4 — This mantra is one of the most quoted and commented-upon in all Upanishadic literature. The identification praṇava = dhanuḥ (OM = bow) makes OM the central meditation technique. The Māṇḍūkya Upanishad is entirely devoted to the analysis of OM, and the Praśna (5.1-7) discusses OM-meditation extensively. The phrase 'śaravat tanmayo bhavet' (like the arrow, become one with That) is the Muṇḍaka's definitive statement of the goal of meditation — not just 'knowing' Brahman but 'becoming' Brahman. This echoes the Muṇḍaka's own later declaration (3.2.9): 'brahma-vid brahmaiva bhavati' — 'the knower of Brahman becomes Brahman.' The word 'apramattena' (with unwavering attention) connects to the Kaṭha (1.3.14): 'uttiṣṭhata jāgrata prāpya varān nibodhata / kṣurasya dhārā niśitā duratyayā durgaṁ pathas tat kavayo vadanti' — 'Arise! Awake! Having obtained excellent teachers, understand. The edge of a razor is sharp and hard to cross — sages say the path is difficult.'

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — OM = धनुष — OM ब्रह्म-विद्या का साधन (means)। आत्मा = शर — तुम स्वयं बाण हो। ब्रह्म = लक्ष्य — एकमात्र लक्ष्य। 'शरवत् तन्मयो भवेत्' = बाण लक्ष्य में जाकर लक्ष्य का ही हो जाता है — आत्मा ब्रह्म-लक्ष्य में जाकर ब्रह्म ही हो जाती है = मोक्ष।
advaita.en: Shankara says OM = bow — OM is the means to brahma-vidyā. Ātmā = arrow — you yourself are the arrow. Brahman = target — the sole target. 'Śaravat tanmayo bhavet' = the arrow enters the target and becomes the target — the Self enters Brahman and becomes Brahman = mokṣa.
advaita.ins: OM is your bow — it gives your meditation its power and direction. You are the arrow — not your thoughts about Brahman, but YOU, your very self. Brahman is the target. And when the arrow hits — you don't bounce back. You merge. Arrow becomes target. Self becomes Brahman. That's liberation.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — OM = धनुष — OM भगवान् के नाम का प्रतीक (symbol of God's name); शर = भक्त-आत्मा (devotee-soul); लक्ष्य = भगवान्। 'तन्मयो भवेत्' = भगवान् में तल्लीन (absorbed in God) — किन्तु ऐक्य (identity) नहीं = सायुज्य (intimate union) — नदी सागर में मिलती है पर जल जल ही रहता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says OM = bow — OM is the symbol of God's name; arrow = the devotee-soul; target = the Lord. 'Tanmayo bhavet' = absorbed in God — but not absolute identity = intimate union (sāyujya) — a river merges into the ocean but water remains water.
vishisht.ins: Chant OM — that's your bow. Offer yourself — that's your arrow. Aim at God — He's your only target. When the arrow reaches God, it doesn't disappear — it rests in God forever. That's sāyujya: the soul at rest in God's presence, absorbed but not annihilated.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — OM = चेतना की एकाग्रता का मन्त्र (mantra of concentration); आत्मा = व्यक्तिगत चेतना (individual consciousness); ब्रह्म = विश्व-चेतना / सच्चिदानन्द। 'तन्मयो भवेत्' = चेतना-रूपान्तर (transformation of consciousness) — व्यक्तिगत → विश्वव्यापी (individual → universal)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says OM = the mantra of concentration; ātmā = individual consciousness; Brahman = universal consciousness / Sat-Chit-Ānanda. 'Tanmayo bhavet' = transformation of consciousness — individual → universal.
aurobindo.ins: OM is the sound that opens the gate. Your consciousness is the arrow that flies through it. And when it reaches the Infinite — it doesn't return. It transforms. Individual consciousness becomes universal consciousness. That's not destruction — it's the expansion you were always meant for.

dp.q: 🔍 OM (praṇava) as the bow — the role of OM in meditation
dp.a: This mantra assigns OM a specific role in the meditation process — it is the bow, the instrument that propels the arrow of the self toward Brahman: Why OM is the bow: (1) The bow provides the framework — the structure within which the arrow operates. OM provides the meditative framework — a point of focus, a sacred sound, a vehicle for concentration. (2) The bow provides the power — the tension that launches the arrow. OM, when chanted with understanding and concentration, generates the inner 'tension' (tapas / spiritual intensity) that launches consciousness toward Brahman. (3) The bow is not the arrow — OM is the means, not the goal. The bow stays behind when the arrow flies. Similarly, OM is the vehicle that carries you toward Brahman, but Brahman itself is beyond OM. OM in the Māṇḍūkya: the Māṇḍūkya Upanishad analyses OM into four parts — A (waking), U (dreaming), M (deep sleep), and the silence beyond (turīya). The entire analysis is designed to show that OM contains and transcends all states of consciousness. OM in the Praśna (5.1-7): the Praśna describes three levels of OM-meditation: (1) meditation on A alone → rebirth in the human world; (2) meditation on A+U → ascent to the moon-world; (3) meditation on A+U+M → realisation of the Puruṣa and liberation. Practical instruction: sit still, chant OM, let the sound become subtler and subtler until it becomes silence, and in that silence, launch your awareness toward the Imperishable. OM is the runway; Brahman is the sky.

dp.q: 🔍 'Tanmayo bhavet' — becoming one with the target
dp.a: The phrase 'śaravat tanmayo bhavet' ('like the arrow, one should become one with That') is the Muṇḍaka's statement of the ultimate goal of meditation: The arrow analogy: when an arrow hits a target with full force, it doesn't bounce back — it embeds itself in the target. The arrow and the target become, in a sense, one unit. Similarly, when consciousness, propelled by OM-meditation, reaches Brahman with full concentration (apramattena), it doesn't 'come back' to ordinary awareness — it merges into Brahman. tanmayaḥ — 'made of That': the compound tat + maya means 'consisting of That' / 'made of That.' The self becomes 'Brahman-constituted.' This is the strongest possible statement of union — not proximity, not similarity, not devotion, but identity of substance. Three interpretations: (1) Advaita: tanmayaḥ = absolute identity. The self IS Brahman and always was; the 'becoming' is the removal of ignorance, not an actual transformation. (2) Viśiṣṭādvaita: tanmayaḥ = intimate union (sāyujya), not absolute identity. The soul rests in God, absorbed in divine bliss, but retains its individuality — as a river merging into the ocean is still water, not ocean. (3) Sri Aurobindo: tanmayaḥ = transformation of consciousness. Individual consciousness doesn't disappear but expands into universal consciousness — the drop becomes the ocean by realising it was always ocean-water. The Muṇḍaka's later echo (3.2.9): 'brahma-vid brahmaiva bhavati' — 'the knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself.' This later verse confirms what this mantra anticipates — the goal is not knowledge about Brahman but becoming Brahman.

sk: यस्मिन्द्यौः पृथिवी चान्तरिक्षमोतं मनः सह प्राणैश्च सर्वैः तमेवैकं जानथ आत्मानमन्या वाचो विमुञ्चथामृतस्यैष सेतुः ||
ro: yasmin · dyauḥ · pṛthivī · ca · antarikṣam · otaṁ · manaḥ · saha · prāṇaiḥ · ca · sarvaiḥ · tam · eva · ekaṁ · jānatha · ātmānam · anyāḥ · vācaḥ · vimuñcatha · amṛtasya · eṣaḥ · setuḥ ||
hi: जिसमें (यस्मिन्) द्यौः (heaven / स्वर्ग), पृथिवी (earth), अन्तरिक्षम् (intermediate space / आकाश) ओतम् (woven / गुँथा हुआ) है — मन (mind) सह सर्वैः प्राणैः (with all the prāṇas / सब प्राणों सहित) — उसी एक (एकम्) आत्मानम् (Self) को जानो (जानथ)! अन्य वाचः (other words / अन्य बातें) विमुञ्चथ (let go / छोड़ दो)! यह (एषः) अमृत (immortality) का सेतु (bridge) है।
en: That in which (yasmin) heaven (dyauḥ), earth (pṛthivī), and the intermediate space (antarikṣam) are woven (otam), [along with] the mind (manas) together with all the prāṇas (saha prāṇaiḥ sarvaiḥ) — know (jānatha) that one (ekam) Self (ātmānam) alone! Let go of (vimuñcatha) other words (anyāḥ vācaḥ)! This (eṣaḥ) is the bridge (setu) to immortality (amṛtasya).

ws.e: woven — from √ve (to weave); heaven, earth, and space are 'woven' into Brahman like threads in a fabric; Brahman is the warp and woof of the cosmos; cf. Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.8.7-8 (Gārgī's question about what the universe is 'woven' on)

ws.h: छोड़ दो / त्याग करो / let go
ws.e: let go / release — vi + √muc (to free/release); a direct command to abandon all other pursuits, all other teachings, all other words; focus on this ONE Self alone
bridge — the Self is the 'bridge' to immortality; a bridge connects two shores — the shore of mortality and the shore of immortality; the Self is the crossing-point
know! — second person plural imperative of √jñā; addressed to all seekers; a collective command — not just 'you' but 'all of you, know!'

ws.h: अन्य बातें / other words / other teachings
ws.e: other words / other speeches — all teachings, discussions, and verbal pursuits that are not about the one Self; the injunction to 'let go' of all other intellectual/verbal activity and focus solely on ātma-jñāna

gr: The command: know the one Self, let go of everything else: this mantra is simultaneously a description, a command, and a promise. otam — 'woven': heaven, earth, and intermediate space are 'woven' into the Self — the cosmos is a fabric and the Self is the thread. This echoes the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (3.8.7-8), where Gārgī asks Yājñavalkya what the universe is 'woven' (ota) on, and the answer is: the akṣara (the Imperishable). anyāḥ vācaḥ vimuñcatha — 'let go of other words': this is a remarkable injunction. The Upanishad — a text of words — is telling you to abandon all words except the one essential teaching: know the Self. All other studies, debates, philosophies, and discussions are to be released. This echoes the Muṇḍaka's earlier distinction between parā and aparā vidyā (1.1.4-5) — aparā (lower knowledge) includes all the Vedas; parā (higher knowledge) is the knowledge of the akṣara alone. amṛtasya eṣaḥ setuḥ — 'this is the bridge to immortality': the Self is a setu (bridge). A bridge does not create the far shore — it only enables you to reach it. The Self is the means of crossing from mortality to immortality.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_2.2.5 — The metaphor of the Self as 'setu' (bridge) to immortality appears also in the Chāndogya (8.4.1-2): 'ātmā vā eṣa setur vidhṛtiḥ' — 'this Self is a bridge, a support.' The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (4.4.22) similarly speaks of the Self as 'setu' — a bridge that holds the worlds apart. The weaving metaphor (otam) is central to the Bṛhadāraṇyaka's third chapter, where Gārgī's questioning culminates in the akṣara as the ultimate 'warp' on which all reality is woven. The injunction 'anyāḥ vācaḥ vimuñcatha' (let go of other words) is radical — it implies that even Vedic learning (aparā vidyā) must be transcended for the sake of ātma-jñāna (parā vidyā).

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'अन्या वाचो विमुञ्चथ' = सब शास्त्र-वाद (scriptural debate), तर्क (logic), और अपरा विद्या छोड़ो — केवल एक आत्मा को जानो। 'सेतुः' = आत्म-ज्ञान = भवसागर (ocean of saṁsāra) पार करने का सेतु (bridge)। 'ओतम्' = सब कुछ आत्मा में ओत-प्रोत (woven) — आत्मा ही अधिष्ठान (substratum)।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'anyāḥ vācaḥ vimuñcatha' = let go of all scriptural debate, logic, and lower knowledge — know only the one Self. 'Setu' = Self-knowledge = the bridge across the ocean of saṁsāra. 'Otam' = everything is woven into the Self — the Self is the substratum.
advaita.ins: Stop debating. Stop accumulating more knowledge. Stop reading more books. There is only one thing to know — the Self. Everything else is woven into it anyway. Know the Self, and you know everything. This knowledge is your bridge across the ocean of death.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'ओतम्' = स्वर्ग, पृथ्वी, अन्तरिक्ष — सब भगवान् में ओत-प्रोत (woven in God)। 'अन्या वाचो विमुञ्चथ' = अन्य उपाय (other means) छोड़ो — भगवान् को जानो = भक्ति-मार्ग (path of devotion)। 'सेतुः' = भगवान् ही अमृत का सेतु — भगवान् के बिना कोई मार्ग नहीं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'otam' = heaven, earth, space — all woven in God. 'Anyāḥ vācaḥ vimuñcatha' = abandon other means — know God = the path of devotion. 'Setu' = God alone is the bridge to immortality — there is no path without God.
vishisht.ins: Everything — heaven, earth, the space between, your mind, your breath — is woven into God like threads in a cloth. Don't chase other paths. Drop other words. God is the only bridge to immortality. Cross it.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'ओतम्' = चेतना वह ताना-बाना (warp and woof) है जिसमें सब लोक, मन, और प्राण बुने हैं। 'अन्या वाचो विमुञ्चथ' = बौद्धिक व्यापार (intellectual activity) छोड़ो — सीधे चेतना में प्रवेश करो। 'सेतुः' = चेतना = मर्त्य (mortal) से अमृत (immortal) तक का सेतु।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'otam' = consciousness is the warp and woof in which all worlds, mind, and prāṇas are woven. 'Anyāḥ vācaḥ vimuñcatha' = abandon intellectual activity — enter consciousness directly. 'Setu' = consciousness = the bridge from mortal to immortal.
aurobindo.ins: The universe is a fabric woven on consciousness. Your mind, your breath, the sky above, the earth below — all threads in one cloth. Stop analyzing the threads. See the cloth. That seeing is the bridge. Cross it, and mortality is behind you.

dp.q: 🔍 'Let go of other words' — the radical demand for focus
dp.a: The command 'anyāḥ vācaḥ vimuñcatha' ('let go of other words') is one of the most radical instructions in the Upanishads: What must be let go? All other teachings, debates, discussions, intellectual pursuits, philosophical arguments — everything that is not the direct knowledge of the one Self. This includes: (1) Aparā vidyā: the 'lower knowledge' — even the four Vedas (Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, Atharva), grammar, etymology, astronomy, etc. These are necessary preparations but must ultimately be transcended. (2) Ritual discussions: debates about the correct performance of sacrifices, the relative merits of different rituals — all of this belongs to karma-kāṇḍa and must be left behind. (3) Philosophical arguments: even intellectual analysis of Brahman — debating whether Brahman is nirguṇa or saguṇa, whether the world is real or illusory — all of this is still 'words' (vācaḥ), not the direct experience. Why this is necessary: words and concepts create a screen between the seeker and reality. As long as you are talking about Brahman, you are not knowing Brahman. Knowledge of Brahman is not verbal — it is the direct 'piercing' described in mantras 3-4. The paradox: this instruction is itself given in words — the Upanishad, a verbal text, is telling you to go beyond words. This is like a finger pointing at the moon — look at the moon, not the finger. The Upanishad points beyond itself.

dp.q: 🔍 The Self as 'setu' (bridge) to immortality
dp.a: The Self is described as a 'setu' (bridge) to immortality (amṛta): What is a bridge? A bridge connects two shores — one where you stand now (mortality, saṁsāra, ignorance) and one you want to reach (immortality, liberation, knowledge). The Self is the bridge between these two conditions. The Chāndogya parallel (8.4.1-2): 'ātmā vā eṣa setur vidhṛtiḥ' — 'This Self is a bridge, a support. Having crossed this bridge, the blind become seeing, the wounded become unwounded, the afflicted become unafflicted. Therefore, having crossed this bridge, night becomes day, for this Brahma-world is ever illuminated.' The Bṛhadāraṇyaka parallel (4.4.22): the Self as 'setu' holds the worlds apart — it is a 'bridge' in the sense of a dam (a barrier that maintains structure), preventing the worlds from collapsing into chaos. Why 'bridge' and not 'boat' or 'path'? A bridge is fixed — it doesn't move. The Self is not a vehicle you ride; it is a structure you cross. It is always there, always available, always stable. You don't need to build it or find it — you need to cross it. The practical implication: the Self is not something you need to acquire — it is something you need to traverse. Self-knowledge is a crossing, not an acquisition.

sk: अरा इव रथनाभौ संहता यत्र नाड्यः स एषोऽन्तश्चरते बहुधा जायमानः ओमित्येवं ध्यायथ आत्मानं स्वस्ति वः पाराय तमसः परस्तात् ||
ro: arāḥ · iva · ratha-nābhau · saṁhatāḥ · yatra · nāḍyaḥ · saḥ · eṣaḥ · antaḥ · carate · bahudhā · jāyamānaḥ · om · iti · evaṁ · dhyāyatha · ātmānaṁ · svasti · vaḥ · pārāya · tamasaḥ · parastāt ||
hi: जैसे अराएँ (spokes) रथ-नाभि (chariot-hub / पहिये की धुरी) में संहत (joined / जुड़ी) हैं — जहाँ नाड़ियाँ (nāḍīs / subtle channels) [मिलती हैं] — वहीं वह (सः एषः) अन्तः चरते (moves within / भीतर विचरता है) — बहुधा जायमानः (being born in many ways / अनेक प्रकार से जन्म लेता हुआ)। OM इति एवं ध्यायथ आत्मानम् (thus meditate on the Self as OM) — स्वस्ति वः (may it be well for you / तुम्हारा कल्याण हो) — पाराय तमसः परस्तात् (for crossing to the far shore beyond darkness / अन्धकार से परे पार जाने के लिए)!
en: Where the subtle channels (nāḍyaḥ) are joined together (saṁhatāḥ) like spokes (arāḥ) in the hub of a chariot-wheel (ratha-nābhau) — there He moves within (antaś carate), being born in many ways (bahudhā jāyamānaḥ). Meditate (dhyāyatha) on the Self (ātmānam) thus — as OM (om iti). May it be well (svasti) for you (vaḥ) for crossing (pārāya) to the far shore, beyond darkness (tamasaḥ parastāt)!

ws.e: spokes — the radial bars of a wheel connecting rim to hub; the nāḍīs (subtle channels) converge on the heart like spokes converge on a hub
the hub of a chariot-wheel — ratha (chariot) + nābhi (navel/hub); the central point where all spokes meet; the heart-centre where all nāḍīs converge
subtle channels — nāḍī = channel/tube in the subtle body; the pathways through which prāṇa flows; traditionally 72,000 nāḍīs originate from the heart

ws.h: अनेक प्रकार से जन्म लेता हुआ / प्रकट होता हुआ
ws.e: being born in many ways — the Self manifests as many functions through the many nāḍīs; one Self, many expressions

ws.h: अन्धकार (tamas) के परे (parastāt) पार (pāra) जाने के लिए
ws.e: for crossing to the far shore beyond darkness — pāra (far shore) + tamas (darkness/ignorance) + parastāt (beyond); the ultimate goal — crossing beyond all darkness/ignorance to the light of immortality

gr: The hub meditation and the blessing: this mantra combines a physiological meditation (the hub of the nāḍīs) with a benediction (svasti vaḥ — 'may it be well for you'). The spoke-hub analogy: the nāḍīs (subtle energy-channels) converge at the heart-centre like spokes converge at the hub of a wheel. The Self 'moves within' this hub — the heart is the operational centre of the Self in the body. bahudhā jāyamānaḥ — 'being born in many ways': the one Self 'manifests' through the many nāḍīs as many functions — sight through the eye-nāḍī, hearing through the ear-nāḍī, etc. The multiplicity of experience is the one Self 'being born many ways.' om iti evaṁ dhyāyatha ātmānam — 'thus meditate on the Self as OM': a direct practical instruction. Meditate on the Self using OM as the focus. svasti vaḥ pārāya tamasaḥ parastāt — 'may it be well for you, for crossing beyond darkness': a teacher's benediction — the teacher wishes the student safe passage across the darkness of ignorance to the far shore of immortality.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_2.2.6 — The spoke-hub image for the nāḍīs converging at the heart appears also in the Praśna (3.6): 'Just as the spokes are fixed in the hub of a wheel, so in this prāṇa everything is fixed.' The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (2.1.19) uses the spider-web variant. The Kaṭha (2.3.17) uses the same image: 'When all the knots of the heart are severed here... the mortal becomes immortal.' The blessing 'svasti vaḥ pārāya tamasaḥ parastāt' echoes the Bṛhadāraṇyaka prayer (1.3.28): 'asato mā sad gamaya, tamaso mā jyotir gamaya, mṛtyor mā amṛtaṁ gamaya' — 'Lead me from darkness to light.' The word 'pāra' (far shore) anticipates the ocean-crossing metaphor of liberation found throughout the Upanishads.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'रथनाभि' = हृदय (heart) — जहाँ नाड़ियाँ अरों (spokes) की भाँति मिलती हैं। आत्मा वहीं 'अन्तः चरते' — हृदय-केन्द्र में। 'बहुधा जायमानः' = एक आत्मा अनेक इन्द्रियों/प्राणों के रूप में प्रकट। 'OM ध्यायथ' = OM ध्यान = सबसे प्रभावी साधन। 'तमसः परस्तात्' = अज्ञान (ignorance) के पार।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'ratha-nābhi' = the heart — where the nāḍīs meet like spokes. The Self 'moves within' there — in the heart-centre. 'Bahudhā jāyamānaḥ' = one Self manifests as many senses/prāṇas. 'OM dhyāyatha' = OM-meditation = the most effective means. 'Tamasaḥ parastāt' = beyond the darkness of ignorance.
advaita.ins: Your heart is a wheel-hub. All your subtle channels radiate from it like spokes. At the centre, the Self sits — one Self, expressing itself through many channels as seeing, hearing, breathing, thinking. Meditate on OM at that centre. Cross beyond the darkness. The teacher is blessing you: 'May it be well.'

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — भगवान् हृदय-कमल (heart-lotus) में विराजमान — नाड़ी-चक्र (wheel of nāḍīs) के केन्द्र में। 'बहुधा जायमानः' = भगवान् अनेक जीवों में अन्तर्यामी (inner controller) रूप में प्रकट। 'स्वस्ति वः' = गुरु का आशीर्वाद (teacher's blessing) — भक्ति-मार्ग पर कल्याण हो।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the Lord resides in the heart-lotus — at the centre of the wheel of nāḍīs. 'Bahudhā jāyamānaḥ' = the Lord manifests as antaryāmī in many beings. 'Svasti vaḥ' = the teacher's blessing — may all be well on the path of devotion.
vishisht.ins: God sits in your heart like a king at the centre of a wheel — every spoke of your being radiates from Him. Meditate on Him as OM. And receive your teacher's blessing: 'May it be well for you — cross beyond the darkness into the light of God.'

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'नाड़ी-नाभि' (hub of nāḍīs) = चेतना का केन्द्रबिन्दु (focal point of consciousness) — हृदय-केन्द्र (heart-centre)। 'बहुधा जायमानः' = एक चेतना — अनेक शक्तियों (powers) में प्रकट। 'तमसः परस्तात्' = अज्ञान-तमस् (darkness of ignorance) = अचेतन (inconscient) — उसके पार = अतिचेतन (superconscient)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'nāḍī-hub' = the focal point of consciousness — the heart-centre. 'Bahudhā jāyamānaḥ' = one consciousness manifesting as many powers. 'Tamasaḥ parastāt' = the darkness of ignorance = the inconscient — beyond it = the superconscient.
aurobindo.ins: All your inner channels converge at one point — the heart-centre. There, one consciousness sits, expressing itself as sight, hearing, thought, breath — many births from one source. Meditate on OM at that point. Cross beyond the darkness of the inconscient into the light of the superconscient.

dp.q: 🔍 The nāḍīs and the heart-centre — the inner geography of the Self
dp.a: This mantra describes the inner geography of the body — the network of nāḍīs (subtle channels) converging at the heart-centre: The nāḍī system: the nāḍīs are subtle energy-channels through which prāṇa (life-force) flows. They are not physical nerves or blood vessels but subtle pathways mapped by yogic experience. Traditional count: the Praśna (3.6) mentions 101 main nāḍīs radiating from the heart; later texts describe 72,000 nāḍīs in total. The hub analogy: the nāḍīs converge at the heart like spokes at a wheel-hub. The heart-centre is the operational headquarters of the Self in the body. All sensory data, all prāṇic flows, all movements of mind converge here. The Praśna parallel (3.6-7): 'From the heart, 101 nāḍīs branch out. From each of these, 100 more. From each of those, 72,000 more. Through these, the vyāna (diffused prāṇa) moves.' The Chāndogya parallel (8.6.6): 'There are 101 channels of the heart. One of these goes up to the crown of the head. Going up by that, one attains immortality.' The meditation instruction: focus awareness at the heart-centre, where all nāḍīs meet. There, the Self sits — one Self, manifesting through many channels as many experiences. Meditate on OM at this point, and cross beyond darkness.

dp.q: 🔍 The teacher's benediction — 'svasti vaḥ' (may it be well for you)
dp.a: The phrase 'svasti vaḥ pārāya tamasaḥ parastāt' ('may it be well for you, for crossing beyond darkness') is a teacher's benediction — a blessing given to students at the culmination of a teaching: What the teacher is doing: the teacher has given the meditation instruction (OM, the bow-and-arrow, the heart-centre). Now the teacher blesses the student — acknowledging that knowledge alone is not sufficient; the student also needs grace, good fortune, and inner strength for the journey. The structure of the blessing: (1) svasti vaḥ = 'may all be well for you' — a general benediction of safety and success. (2) pārāya = 'for crossing' — the spiritual journey as a crossing, an ocean-voyage, a bridge-traversal. (3) tamasaḥ parastāt = 'beyond the darkness' — the destination: beyond all ignorance, beyond all suffering, beyond mortality. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka's great prayer (1.3.28): 'tamaso mā jyotir gamaya' — 'Lead me from darkness to light.' The Muṇḍaka's teacher is not just praying for this but blessing the student to achieve it. The emotional weight: this is one of the rare moments in the Upanishads where the teacher steps out of the role of instructor and into the role of well-wisher. The teacher cares about the student — not just intellectually but personally. 'May it be well for you.' The tenderness of 'somya' returns.

sk: यः सर्वज्ञः सर्वविद्यस्य ज्ञानमयं तपः तस्मादेतद्ब्रह्म नामरूपमन्नं च जायते ||
ro: yaḥ · sarva-jñaḥ · sarva-vit · yasya · jñāna-mayaṁ · tapaḥ · tasmāt · etat · brahma · nāma-rūpam · annaṁ · ca · jāyate ||
hi: जो सर्वज्ञ (omniscient / सब-जानने वाला) है, सर्ववित् (all-knowing / सब कुछ का ज्ञाता) है, जिसका तपस् (creative austerity / सृष्टि-तप) ज्ञानमय (consisting of knowledge / ज्ञान-स्वरूप) है — उससे (तस्मात्) यह ब्रह्म (Vedic reality / ब्रह्मा / Hiraṇyagarbha), नाम-रूप (name and form), और अन्न (food / matter) जायते (is born / उत्पन्न होता है)।
en: He who is omniscient (sarva-jña), all-knowing (sarva-vit), whose tapas (creative austerity) consists of knowledge (jñāna-maya) — from Him are born this Brahman (the Vedic reality / Hiraṇyagarbha), name-and-form (nāma-rūpa), and food (anna).

ws.e: omniscient — sarva (all) + jña (knowing); He knows everything in general; the comprehensive knowledge of the whole

ws.h: सब कुछ का विशेष ज्ञाता / all-knowing in detail
ws.e: all-knowing — sarva (all) + vit (knowing in detail); while sarva-jña = general omniscience, sarva-vit = detailed knowledge of every particular; together they cover universal and particular knowledge

ws.h: ज्ञान-स्वरूप तप / austerity consisting of knowledge
ws.e: creative austerity consisting of knowledge — Brahman's tapas is not physical exertion but pure knowing; creation arises from knowledge, not from effort

ws.h: नाम और रूप / name and form
ws.e: name and form — the two aspects that differentiate one object from another; individuation; the principle of diversity in creation; cf. Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.7 and Chāndogya 6.3.2-3
food / matter — anna literally means 'food' but in Vedāntic cosmology also represents the material substrate; cf. Taittirīya 2.2.1: 'From food, all beings are born'

gr: Brahman's knowledge-tapas as the source of creation: this mantra returns to the theme of creation but with a crucial specification — Brahman's tapas (creative energy) is jñāna-maya (consisting of knowledge). sarva-jña vs. sarva-vit: two kinds of knowing are attributed to Brahman: sarva-jña (omniscient — knowing the whole) and sarva-vit (all-knowing — knowing every detail). Together they affirm that Brahman's knowledge is both comprehensive and particular — nothing escapes it, in general or in detail. jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ — 'tapas consisting of knowledge': Brahman does not create through effort, labour, or material processing. Brahman creates through knowing. Knowledge itself is the creative force. This is a profound theological claim — consciousness (jñāna) is not a passive mirror but an active creative power. brahma, nāma-rūpa, anna: from Brahman's knowledge-tapas emerge three things: (1) brahma — the first-born reality (Hiraṇyagarbha / the cosmic mind), (2) nāma-rūpa — name and form (the principle of individuation), (3) anna — food/matter (the physical substrate). This covers the hierarchy of creation from subtle (brahma) through intermediate (nāma-rūpa) to gross (anna).
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_2.2.7 — This mantra echoes Muṇḍaka 1.1.9: 'yaḥ sarva-jñaḥ sarva-vit yasya jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ' — the same phrase appears in both, creating a structural echo between the first and second Muṇḍakas. The distinction sarva-jña / sarva-vit is discussed by Shankara: sarva-jña = sāmānya-jñāna (general knowledge), sarva-vit = viśeṣa-jñāna (particular knowledge). The term 'nāma-rūpa' (name and form) is central to Vedāntic philosophy — it appears prominently in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (1.4.7: 'He entered here to the very tips of the nails, as a razor is hidden in a razor-case... This Self entered these bodies up to the tips of the nails. People do not see Him, for He is incomplete... He is called nāma-rūpa') and the Chāndogya (6.3.2-3: the tripartite creation of fire, water, earth through nāma-rūpa). The triad brahma-nāmarūpa-anna parallels the Taittirīya's five-sheath model in compressed form.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'ज्ञानमयं तपः' = ब्रह्म का तप = ज्ञान-स्वरूप — शारीरिक तप नहीं। सृष्टि = ब्रह्म के ज्ञान (knowledge) से उत्पन्न — सङ्कल्प-मात्र (mere willing/knowing) से। 'नामरूप' = माया (illusion) — अध्यास (superimposition) — ब्रह्म पर आरोपित।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ' = Brahman's tapas = knowledge-constituted — not physical austerity. Creation = produced by Brahman's knowledge — by mere willing/knowing. 'Nāma-rūpa' = māyā (illusion) — superimposed on Brahman.
advaita.ins: Brahman doesn't build the universe — Brahman thinks it. The creative power is knowledge itself, not effort. And what emerges — names, forms, matter — are the dream-shapes of Brahman's infinite knowing. The universe is a thought thinking itself.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'सर्वज्ञः सर्ववित्' = भगवान् सर्वज्ञ — सामान्य और विशेष दोनों ज्ञान। 'ज्ञानमयं तपः' = भगवान् की सृष्टि-शक्ति (creative power) = ज्ञान और सङ्कल्प (will)। 'नामरूप' = वास्तविक (real) विविधता — माया नहीं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'sarva-jña sarva-vit' = the Lord is omniscient — both general and particular knowledge. 'Jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ' = the Lord's creative power = knowledge and will. 'Nāma-rūpa' = real diversity — not māyā/illusion.
vishisht.ins: God knows everything — the whole picture and every detail. And His creative power is His knowledge itself. He doesn't struggle to create — He knows things into being. Names, forms, and matter flow from His omniscient will.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'ज्ञानमयं तपः' = चेतना की सृजनात्मक शक्ति (creative power of consciousness) = तप-शक्ति (tapas-force)। सृष्टि = चेतना (consciousness) + शक्ति (force) का संयोग — ज्ञान ही शक्ति है। 'नामरूप' = चेतना के प्रतिरूप (patterns of consciousness)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ' = the creative power of consciousness = tapas-force. Creation = the union of consciousness + force — knowledge itself is power. 'Nāma-rūpa' = patterns of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: Knowledge is not passive — it creates. Consciousness is not a mirror — it's a forge. Brahman knows, and that knowing IS the creative fire. Names, forms, and matter are the patterns that emerge from consciousness working upon itself.

dp.q: 🔍 'Jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ' — creation through knowledge, not effort
dp.a: The phrase 'jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ' ('tapas consisting of knowledge') makes a profound claim about the nature of creation: What is tapas? Ordinarily, tapas means 'austerity' — physical or mental effort, discipline, heat. In Vedic cosmology, tapas is the creative energy — the universe is created through the tapas of the creator. But Brahman's tapas is knowledge: the Muṇḍaka specifies that Brahman's tapas is not physical effort but jñāna-maya — consisting of knowledge. Brahman doesn't 'work' to create the universe — Brahman knows it into existence. Knowledge itself is the creative force. The philosophical significance: if creation comes from knowledge (not from effort or material), then: (1) Consciousness is primary: the universe is born from consciousness, not from matter. Matter is a product of consciousness, not the other way around. (2) Knowledge is power: knowing IS creating. This connects to the modern insight that 'information' may be more fundamental than matter or energy. (3) Creation is effortless: Brahman doesn't strain to create — it is as natural as knowing. Just as you don't 'work' to think a thought, Brahman doesn't 'work' to produce the universe. The Taittirīya parallel (2.6.1): 'so'kāmayata — bahu syāṁ prajāyeya' — 'He desired: may I become many, may I be born.' The desire (kāma) that creates is a form of knowledge — Brahman 'knows' what it wants to become.

dp.q: 🔍 Nāma-rūpa — the principle of individuation
dp.a: The term nāma-rūpa ('name and form') is one of the most important concepts in Vedāntic philosophy: What is nāma-rūpa? Nāma (name) = the conceptual identity of a thing — what makes a 'table' a table, a 'tree' a tree. Rūpa (form) = the sensory appearance — the shape, colour, texture that distinguish one thing from another. Together, nāma-rūpa = the principle of individuation — what makes the one Brahman appear as many separate objects. The Chāndogya's teaching (6.1.4-6): Uddālaka tells Śvetaketu: 'All modification is a verbal distinction, a name — the reality is just clay.' A pot, a plate, and a brick are all 'clay' — the differences are nāma-rūpa (name and form). Similarly, the entire universe is Brahman — the differences are nāma-rūpa. Three views: (1) Advaita: nāma-rūpa = māyā — the apparent (not real) differences superimposed on the one Brahman. The universe of names and forms is like a dream — real while it lasts but dissolving upon awakening. (2) Viśiṣṭādvaita: nāma-rūpa = real modifications (pariṇāma) of Brahman's body. The diversity is real, not illusory — but all of it is Brahman's self-expression. (3) Sri Aurobindo: nāma-rūpa = the self-determining patterns of consciousness. Consciousness shapes itself into distinct forms — not as illusion but as creative play (līlā).

sk: तदेतत्सत्यं मन्त्रेषु कर्माणि कवयो यान्यपश्यंस्तानि त्रेतायां बहुधा सन्ततानि तान्याचरथ नियतं सत्यकामा एष वः पन्थाः सुकृतस्य लोके ||
ro: tat · etat · satyam · mantreṣu · karmāṇi · kavayaḥ · yāni · apaśyan · tāni · tretāyāṁ · bahudhā · santatāni · tāni · ācaratha · niyataṁ · satya-kāmāḥ · eṣaḥ · vaḥ · panthāḥ · su-kṛtasya · loke ||
hi: वह यह सत्य (truth) है। मन्त्रों (Vedic mantras) में कवियों (seers / ऋषियों) ने जो कर्माणि (ritual actions) अपश्यन् (saw / देखे) — वे त्रेतायाम् (in the Tretā / three Vedic fires) बहुधा सन्ततानि (spread out in many ways / विविध रूप से फैलाए गए) हैं। हे सत्यकामाः (lovers of truth / सत्य-प्रेमियों)! तानि आचरथ नियतम् (practise them regularly / उन्हें नियमपूर्वक आचरण करो)! यह (एषः) तुम्हारा (वः) पन्थाः (path / मार्ग) है — सुकृतस्य लोके (in the world of good deeds / पुण्य-लोक में)।
en: This is the truth (satyam). The ritual actions (karmāṇi) that the seers (kavayaḥ) saw (apaśyan) in the mantras — those are spread out (santatāni) in many ways (bahudhā) in the Tretā (the three Vedic fires). Practise them (ācaratha) regularly (niyatam), O lovers of truth (satya-kāmāḥ)! This (eṣaḥ) is your (vaḥ) path (panthāḥ) in the world of good deeds (sukṛtasya loke).

ws.e: seers / sages — kavi = seer/poet; the Vedic ṛṣis who 'saw' the mantras; they did not compose the Vedas but perceived them through spiritual vision
in the Tretā — the three Vedic sacrificial fires: gārhapatya (household fire), āhavanīya (offering fire), dakṣiṇāgni (southern fire); the ritual system based on three fires
spread out / extended — from sam + √tan (to stretch); the ritual actions are elaborated in many forms across the Vedic corpus

ws.h: सत्य-प्रेमी / सत्य की कामना वाले / lovers of truth
ws.e: lovers of truth — satya (truth) + kāma (desire/love); those who desire truth; an address to qualified students; cf. Chāndogya 4.4: Satyakāma Jābāla
path / way — the path of karma (ritual action) that leads to the world of good deeds; distinguished from the higher path of jñāna (knowledge) leading to Brahman

gr: The integration of karma-mārga within the larger framework: after the soaring meditation teachings (bow-and-arrow, OM, the heart-centre), this mantra returns to the ritual path (karma-mārga) — but now seen within its proper context. The apparent contradiction: the Muṇḍaka earlier critiqued rituals as 'leaky boats' (1.2.7). Now it says 'practise them' (ācaratha). This is not a contradiction — the critique was of rituals as sole means to liberation; here they are presented as a valid path (panthāḥ) to the 'world of good deeds' (sukṛtasya loke) — a worldly, not ultimate, goal. satya-kāmāḥ — 'lovers of truth': the address implies that the ritual path is for those who genuinely seek truth — not for the deluded (mūḍhāḥ) who mistake rituals for the ultimate (as in 1.2). kavayaḥ apaśyan — 'the seers saw': the rituals were not invented but seen (apaśyan) by the seers — they have cosmic authority.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_2.2.8_note — This mantra (2.2.8) appears to interrupt the flow of the jñāna-kāṇḍa (knowledge section) with a return to karma (ritual action). Some commentators interpret this as an interpolation; others see it as a deliberate integration — the Muṇḍaka acknowledges the validity of karma-mārga within its proper sphere (punya/merit) while maintaining that the ultimate path is jñāna. The term 'tretā' (three fires) connects to the 'three fires' (trayo agnayaḥ) of 1.2.1 — the same ritual system that was critiqued is now given its proper place. The address 'satya-kāmāḥ' (lovers of truth) parallels the Chāndogya's famous student Satyakāma Jābāla (4.4) — suggesting that even the karma path requires sincerity and truth-seeking.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — यह कर्म-मार्ग (path of action) की स्तुति नहीं — उचित-स्थान-निर्धारण (proper placement) है। कर्म = पुण्य-लोक (world of merit) तक ले जाता है — ब्रह्म-लोक (Brahman-world) तक नहीं। 'सुकृतस्य लोके' = सुकृत (good deeds) का लोक — मोक्ष नहीं।
advaita.en: Shankara says this is not praise of the karma path — it is proper placement. Karma leads to the world of merit (sukṛtasya loke) — not to Brahman-realisation. 'Sukṛtasya loke' = the world of good deeds — not mokṣa.
advaita.ins: The ritual path isn't wrong — it's limited. It takes you to the world of good deeds — a better world, but still a world. If you want the ultimate, you need the arrow of knowledge. But if you're a lover of truth, start where you are — even ritual practice, done with sincerity, is a step on the path.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — कर्म-मार्ग = उपासना (worship) और भक्ति (devotion) के साथ मिलकर = मोक्ष-मार्ग का अंग। 'सत्यकामाः' = सत्य-प्रेमी = भगवान्-प्रेमी। 'आचरथ' = वैदिक कर्म भगवान् की आराधना (worship of God) के रूप में करो।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says karma path = combined with upāsanā (worship) and bhakti (devotion) = a component of the path to liberation. 'Satya-kāmāḥ' = lovers of truth = lovers of God. 'Ācaratha' = perform Vedic rituals as worship of God.
vishisht.ins: Rituals aren't empty — they're acts of worship when done with love for God. The seers saw these practices in vision. Perform them with devotion, with truth as your desire. This is your path — not the ultimate path alone, but a real path that prepares the heart for God.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'कर्माणि' = चेतना के बाह्य अनुष्ठान (external rituals of consciousness)। ये 'कवियों' ने 'देखे' — अन्तर्दृष्टि (inner vision) से। 'सत्यकामाः' = सत्य-अभीप्सु (aspirants of truth)। कर्म-मार्ग = यात्रा का आरम्भ — अन्तिम लक्ष्य (ultimate goal) ज्ञान (knowledge) है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'karmāṇi' = external rituals of consciousness. These were 'seen' by the seers through inner vision. 'Satya-kāmāḥ' = aspirants of truth. Karma-path = the beginning of the journey — the ultimate goal is knowledge.
aurobindo.ins: The rituals are real — the seers saw them as patterns of consciousness. Practise them, lovers of truth, but know what they are: the outer gesture pointing to the inner reality. They pave the path through the world of good deeds. The arrow of knowledge completes the journey.

dp.q: 🔍 Reconciling the ritual critique (1.2) with the ritual endorsement (2.2.8)
dp.a: This mantra seems to contradict the Muṇḍaka's earlier harsh critique of ritual (1.2.7-10: 'leaky boats,' 'the blind leading the blind'). How to reconcile? The resolution: the critique in 1.2 was of rituals as the sole means to liberation — as if ritual performance alone could confer mokṣa. That is what the Muṇḍaka rejects. Here in 2.2.8: rituals are acknowledged as valid within their sphere — they lead to 'sukṛtasya loke' (the world of good deeds) — a reward, but not the ultimate reward. The rituals are not dismissed as useless; they are placed in their proper position within a hierarchy: (1) Karma (rituals) → leads to better births, heavenly worlds, merit — but these are exhaustible (kṣīṇa-loke, 1.2.9). (2) Upāsanā (meditation on OM, bow-and-arrow) → leads to gradual liberation (krama-mukti). (3) Jñāna (direct knowledge of Brahman) → leads to immediate liberation (sadyo-mukti / jīvan-mukti). The Muṇḍaka's balanced view: rituals are not wrong — they are limited. For 'lovers of truth' (satya-kāmāḥ), they are a valid starting point. The error is in treating the starting point as the destination.

dp.q: 🔍 The seers as 'viewers' of ritual — 'kavayaḥ apaśyan'
dp.a: The phrase 'kavayaḥ yāni apaśyan' ('the seers saw') makes an important claim about the origin of Vedic rituals: The seers did not invent: the word 'apaśyan' (they saw) implies that the rituals were not humanly invented or composed. They were perceived through spiritual vision — the seers 'saw' the rituals as patterns in the cosmic order, just as they 'saw' the mantras. The Vedic tradition's self-understanding: the Vedas (including the ritual instructions) are apauruṣeya — 'not of human authorship.' They are eternal truths perceived by the ṛṣis in states of heightened consciousness. The rituals are therefore not arbitrary cultural practices but cosmic laws — as real and as binding as the laws of physics. The implication: if the rituals were 'seen' by seers, they have authority — they work. The Muṇḍaka never denies that rituals work. It only denies that they work for liberation. They work for what they promise — better births, heavenly worlds, merit — but their scope is limited. The connection to jñāna: the same seers (kavayaḥ) who 'saw' the rituals also 'saw' the higher truth. The two levels of knowledge — ritual (aparā) and Self-knowledge (parā) — were both perceived by the same ṛṣis. The seers did not choose one over the other; they saw the whole picture.

sk: यदा चर्मवदाकाशं वेष्टयिष्यन्ति मानवाः तदा देवमविज्ञाय दुःखस्यान्तो भविष्यति ||
ro: yadā · carma-vat · ākāśaṁ · veṣṭayiṣyanti · mānvāḥ · tadā · devam · avijñāya · duḥkhasya · antaḥ · bhaviṣyati ||
hi: जब (यदा) मानव (mānvāḥ / मनुष्य) आकाश (space) को चर्म-वत् (like a hide / चमड़े की तरह) वेष्टयिष्यन्ति (will roll up / लपेट लेंगे) — तब (तदा) देवम् (the Divine / दिव्य पुरुष / God) को अविज्ञाय (without knowing / बिना जाने) दुःख का अन्त (end of suffering) भविष्यति (will be / होगा)।
en: When (yadā) humans (mānavāḥ) will roll up (veṣṭayiṣyanti) space (ākāśam) like a hide (carma-vat) — then (tadā), without knowing (avijñāya) the Divine (devam), there will be (bhaviṣyati) an end (antaḥ) to suffering (duḥkhasya).

ws.h: चमड़े की तरह / like a leather hide
ws.e: like a hide — carma (skin/leather) + vat (like); a leather hide can be rolled up; but space cannot — this is the impossible condition
space — the most pervading of the five elements; it cannot be rolled up; this describes an impossibility
will roll up — future tense of √veṣṭ (to wrap/roll); a deliberately impossible action — no one can roll up space

ws.h: बिना जाने / बिना ज्ञान के / without knowing
ws.e: without knowing — a + vijñāya (having known); the crucial gerund — 'without knowing God' = the condition that makes suffering's end impossible
end of suffering — duḥkha (suffering/pain/sorrow) + anta (end); the goal of all spiritual seeking — the cessation of suffering

gr: The impossible condition — a reductio ad absurdum: this mantra uses a rhetorical impossibility to make an absolute claim. The structure: 'When X (impossible) happens, THEN Y (end of suffering without God-knowledge) will happen.' Since X can never happen (you cannot roll up infinite space like a leather hide), Y can also never happen. Therefore: there is no end to suffering without knowing God. The logic: (1) Rolling up space = impossible. (2) Ending suffering without knowing God = equally impossible. (3) Therefore: God-knowledge is the ONLY way to end suffering — there is no alternative path, no shortcut, no workaround. Why 'rolling up space'? Space (ākāśa) is the most pervading, most intangible, most unfoldable of all things. You cannot grasp it, contain it, or roll it up. The image is chosen for maximum impossibility — if someone asks 'can suffering end without knowing God?' the answer is: only when you can roll up the sky like a bedsheet. The Śvetāśvatara parallel (6.20): the Śvetāśvatara uses the same image but in a positive sense — 'only by knowing God does one transcend sorrow.'
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_2.2.9 — This mantra is virtually identical to Śvetāśvatara 6.20: 'yadā carmavad ākāśaṁ veṣṭayiṣyanti mānavāḥ / tadā devam avijñāya duḥkhasyānto bhaviṣyati.' The shared text suggests either borrowing or a common source. The Śvetāśvatara (which has Shaiva tendencies) uses 'deva' to refer to Śiva/Rudra; the Muṇḍaka's 'deva' is identified by Shankara with the nirguṇa Brahman and by Ramanuja with Nārāyaṇa. The rhetorical device — stating an impossibility as a condition for another impossibility — is called 'adṛṣṭānta' (impossible illustration) and is a powerful form of Vedic rhetoric. The Muṇḍaka's point is unambiguous: knowledge of God is the ONLY path to the end of suffering. No other path — karma, ritual, worldly knowledge — will suffice.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'आकाशं चर्मवत् वेष्टयिष्यन्ति' = असम्भव (impossible)। वैसे ही 'देवम् अविज्ञाय दुःखस्यान्तः' = असम्भव। ज्ञान (knowledge) के बिना दुःख-निवृत्ति (end of suffering) = कभी सम्भव नहीं। कर्म, तप, दान — कुछ भी ज्ञान का विकल्प (substitute) नहीं।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'rolling up space like a hide' = impossible. Likewise 'ending suffering without knowing God' = impossible. Ending suffering without knowledge = never possible. Karma, tapas, charity — nothing substitutes for knowledge.
advaita.ins: Can you roll up the sky like a blanket? No? Then you can't end suffering without knowing the Divine. It's that absolute. No ritual, no austerity, no charity, no worldly achievement will end your deepest suffering. Only knowledge of the Divine. Only that.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'देवम् अविज्ञाय' = भगवान् को बिना जाने / बिना भक्ति के। भगवान् का ज्ञान = भक्ति-ज्ञान (devotional knowledge) = दुःख-निवृत्ति का एकमात्र उपाय (sole means)। आकाश को लपेटना जितना असम्भव — उतना ही असम्भव भगवान् बिना मुक्ति।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'devam avijñāya' = without knowing God / without devotion. Knowledge of God = devotional knowledge = the sole means to end suffering. Rolling up space is as impossible as liberation without God.
vishisht.ins: You can try every path — rituals, austerities, philosophies — but without knowing God, suffering won't end. It's as impossible as rolling up the sky. God-knowledge is not one option among many. It's the ONLY option. Everything else is rearranging furniture in a burning house.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'देवम् अविज्ञाय' = दिव्य चेतना (divine consciousness) को बिना जाने। दुःख = अज्ञान (ignorance) का परिणाम — अज्ञान = चेतना से विच्छेद (disconnection from consciousness)। चेतना को जानना = दुःख से मुक्ति — कोई विकल्प नहीं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'devam avijñāya' = without knowing divine consciousness. Suffering = the result of ignorance — ignorance = disconnection from consciousness. Knowing consciousness = freedom from suffering — no alternative.
aurobindo.ins: Suffering exists because you're disconnected from your own divine nature. No external remedy can fix an internal disconnection. You can't roll up space — and you can't end suffering without reconnecting with the Divine. That reconnection IS the end of suffering.

dp.q: 🔍 The impossible condition — rhetoric of absolute necessity
dp.a: The impossible condition ('when humans roll up space like a hide') is a powerful rhetorical device: How it works: the mantra states an impossible condition (rolling up space) and makes an impossible consequence depend on it (ending suffering without God-knowledge). Since the condition can never be met, the consequence can never occur. The logic is: 'suffering will end without knowing God when, and only when, space can be rolled up like a hide — i.e., NEVER.' Why this device? It conveys absolute necessity. Not 'knowing God is helpful for ending suffering' or 'knowing God is the best way to end suffering' but: knowing God is the ONLY way to end suffering — period. There is no alternative, no workaround, no exception. The image of 'rolling up space': space (ākāśa) is the most pervading, most intangible, most uncontainable of all things. It cannot be grasped, folded, or wrapped. You might imagine rolling up earth (a map), or rolling up water (a scroll), but space itself?
