The impossibility is so extreme that it borders on the absurd — which is precisely the point. The practical takeaway: stop looking for alternatives. Stop hoping that enough merit, enough practice, enough worldly success will eventually end suffering. Only one thing ends suffering: knowing the Divine. Start there.

dp.q: 🔍 The Śvetāśvatara parallel and the identity of 'deva'
dp.a: This mantra is virtually identical to Śvetāśvatara 6.20, raising interesting questions about the identity of 'deva' (the Divine): The shared text: 'yadā carmavad ākāśaṁ veṣṭayiṣyanti mānavāḥ / tadā devam avijñāya duḥkhasyānto bhaviṣyati' — the wording is identical in both Upanishads. Who is 'deva'? (1) In the Śvetāśvatara: the Śvetāśvatara has Shaiva tendencies — 'deva' there is identified with Rudra/Śiva, the personal God who is both immanent and transcendent. (2) In the Muṇḍaka (Shankara's reading): 'deva' = the nirguṇa Brahman — the impersonal Absolute that is beyond all attributes but shines (√div = to shine) by its own light. (3) In the Muṇḍaka (Ramanuja's reading): 'deva' = Nārāyaṇa / Viṣṇu — the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). (4) In Sri Aurobindo's reading: 'deva' = the divine consciousness — the supramental reality that transcends and includes all personal and impersonal aspects. The convergence: despite doctrinal differences, all interpreters agree on the essential message: without knowledge of the ultimate reality (by whatever name), suffering cannot end. The disagreement is about the nature of that reality, not about its necessity.

sk: तपसा चीयते ब्रह्म ततोऽन्नमभिजायते अन्नात्प्राणो मनः सत्यं लोकाः कर्मसु चामृतम् ||
ro: tapasā · cīyate · brahma · tataḥ · annam · abhijāyate · annāt · prāṇaḥ · manaḥ · satyaṁ · lokāḥ · karmasu · ca · amṛtam ||
hi: तपसा (by tapas / तप से) ब्रह्म (Brahman / Vedic reality) चीयते (is built up / accumulated / संचित होता है)। ततः (from that) अन्नम् (food / matter) अभिजायते (is born / उत्पन्न होता है)। अन्न से प्राण (life-breath), मनः (mind), सत्यम् (truth), लोकाः (worlds), और कर्मसु अमृतम् (in actions, immortality / कर्मों में अमरत्व) [उत्पन्न होते हैं]।
en: By tapas (austerity/creative energy), Brahman is built up (cīyate); from that, food/matter (anna) is born (abhijāyate). From food [come] prāṇa (life-breath), manas (mind), truth (satya), the worlds (lokāḥ), and immortality in actions (karmasu amṛtam).

ws.h: संचित होता है / accumulated / built up
ws.e: is built up / accumulated — from √ci (to pile up/accumulate); the same root used for building the fire-altar (citi/cayana); Brahman is 'built up' through tapas as the fire-altar is built brick by brick
is born / springs forth — abhi + √jan (to be born); food/matter springs forth from Brahman after Brahman is 'built up' by tapas

ws.h: कर्मों में अमरत्व / immortality in works
ws.e: immortality in actions — the immortal element within karmic activity; the fruit of tapas extends into the realm of action and makes even actions a vehicle for the imperishable

gr: The creation-sequence through tapas: this mantra traces a compact creation-sequence: tapas → Brahman → anna (food/matter) → prāṇa → manas → satya → lokāḥ → amṛta in karma. tapasā cīyate brahma — 'by tapas, Brahman is built up': the verb 'cīyate' (from √ci, to pile up) is the technical term for building the Vedic fire-altar (agni-cayana). The image is striking — Brahman is 'accumulated' or 'built up' through tapas, as a fire-altar is built brick by brick. This may mean: (1) Brahman's creative potential is activated through tapas, or (2) the aspirant's realisation of Brahman is 'built up' through sustained tapas. The descent from Brahman to matter to life to mind: Brahman → anna (matter/food) → prāṇa (life) → manas (mind) → satya (truth) → lokāḥ (worlds) → amṛta (immortality in karma). This is a compact version of the Taittirīya's pañcakośa (five-sheath) model. karmasu amṛtam — 'immortality in actions': even within the realm of karma (action), there is a dimension of immortality. Actions performed with knowledge and tapas carry an imperishable element — they are not merely finite deeds but expressions of the eternal.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_2.2.10 — The creation-sequence (tapas → brahma → anna → prāṇa → manas → satya → lokāḥ → karmasu amṛtam) is a compressed parallel to the Taittirīya's creation-sequence (2.1.1): 'From this Self, space was born; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth; from earth, herbs; from herbs, food; from food, the person.' The word 'cīyate' (is built up) connects to the agni-cayana (fire-altar construction) ritual described in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa — the most elaborate of all Vedic rituals, in which the fire-altar is built in the shape of a bird (a symbol of the Self's flight to immortality). The phrase 'karmasu amṛtam' (immortality in actions) is notable — it suggests that even the karma-mārga, when informed by tapas and knowledge, participates in the imperishable.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'तपसा चीयते ब्रह्म' = तप से ब्रह्म-ज्ञान (knowledge of Brahman) 'संचित' (accumulated) होता है — ज्ञान एक ही बार में नहीं — क्रमिक (gradual) प्रक्रिया। अन्न → प्राण → मन → सत्य → लोक = सृष्टि-क्रम (creation-order)। 'कर्मसु अमृतम्' = ज्ञान-युक्त कर्म (knowledge-informed action) में भी अमृत-अंश (element of immortality) है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'tapasā cīyate brahma' = through tapas, knowledge of Brahman is 'accumulated' — knowledge is not instant but gradual. Anna → prāṇa → manas → satya → lokāḥ = the creation-order. 'Karmasu amṛtam' = even in knowledge-informed action there is an element of immortality.
advaita.ins: Knowledge of Brahman isn't a lightning bolt — it's a fire you build, brick by brick, through sustained practice (tapas). And from that knowledge, everything flows: life, mind, truth, worlds, and even immortality within action. Build the fire patiently. The whole universe is in the flame.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'तपसा चीयते ब्रह्म' = तप (austerity/devotion) से भगवान् की कृपा (grace) प्राप्त होती है — भगवान् 'चीयते' = भक्त के हृदय में 'निर्मित' होते हैं। भगवान् से अन्न → प्राण → मन → सत्य → लोक → अमृत — सम्पूर्ण सृष्टि।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'tapasā cīyate brahma' = through tapas (austerity/devotion), God's grace is obtained — God is 'built up' in the devotee's heart. From God: anna → prāṇa → manas → satya → lokāḥ → amṛta — the complete creation.
vishisht.ins: Through devotion and discipline, God grows in your heart — like a fire-altar built brick by brick. And from that inner God, everything flows: life, mind, truth, worlds, and immortality even in your daily actions. Build the altar of devotion. God will fill it with everything.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'तपसा चीयते ब्रह्म' = चेतना-शक्ति (consciousness-force = tapas) से चेतना (consciousness = brahma) स्वयं को 'निर्मित' करती है — विकसित (evolve) करती है। अन्न → प्राण → मन = चेतना का क्रमिक अवतरण (progressive descent)। 'कर्मसु अमृतम्' = क्रिया (action) में भी चेतना का अमर अंश है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'tapasā cīyate brahma' = through consciousness-force (tapas), consciousness (brahma) builds itself up — evolves itself. Anna → prāṇa → manas = the progressive descent of consciousness. 'Karmasu amṛtam' = even in action, there is an immortal element of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: Consciousness builds itself through its own energy — tapas is consciousness in action. It descends: first as matter, then life, then mind, then truth, then whole worlds. And even in your everyday actions, there's an imperishable spark. Nothing you do is entirely mortal — because consciousness is immortal, and you are consciousness.

dp.q: 🔍 'Cīyate' — Brahman built like a fire-altar
dp.a: The verb 'cīyate' (is built up / accumulated) comes from √ci — the same root used for the most elaborate of all Vedic rituals, the agni-cayana (fire-altar construction): The agni-cayana: this is a massive ritual in which a fire-altar is constructed in the shape of a bird (śyena) from 10,800 bricks, over the course of a year. Each brick is laid with specific mantras; the entire structure represents the universe, time, and the Self's flight to immortality. The metaphor: just as the fire-altar is 'built up' (cīyate) brick by brick, Brahman-knowledge is 'built up' through sustained tapas — discipline, study, meditation, practice. It is not a sudden flash but a gradual construction. The implication: spiritual realisation requires patient, persistent effort — like building an altar one brick at a time. Each meditation is a brick. Each act of discipline is a brick. Each insight is a brick. Over time, the altar rises — and the fire of knowledge blazes upon it. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (10.2.3.1-5): describes the agni-cayana as a re-creation of the self — 'the sacrificer, having built up the fire-altar, builds up himself.' The altar IS the self. Building the altar IS building the self. Similarly: 'tapasā cīyate brahma' = through tapas, one builds up Brahman-realisation within oneself.

dp.q: 🔍 'Karmasu amṛtam' — immortality within action
dp.a: The phrase 'karmasu amṛtam' ('immortality in actions') is a remarkable conclusion: What it means: even within the realm of karma (action/ritual), there is an element of immortality (amṛta). Actions are not merely finite, transient deeds — when informed by tapas and knowledge, they carry an imperishable dimension. Three interpretations: (1) Advaita: actions performed with knowledge (jñāna-karma) have an 'immortal' element because the doer (ātman) is itself immortal. When you act knowing 'I am Brahman,' your actions are not binding — they are expressions of the immortal Self. (2) Viśiṣṭādvaita: actions performed as worship (bhagavad-ārādhana) participate in the Lord's immortality. When you offer every action to God, even ordinary deeds become vehicles of the eternal. (3) Sri Aurobindo: every action is an expression of consciousness (which is immortal). Even in the densest, most material action, the spark of consciousness is present — and that spark is amṛta. The Bhagavad Gītā connection (3.19): 'Therefore, without attachment, perform action that ought to be done; for by performing action without attachment, one attains the Supreme.' The Gītā's karma-yoga — action without attachment — is one interpretation of 'karmasu amṛtam.' The practical takeaway: your actions can be vehicles for immortality — but only when informed by knowledge and tapas. Otherwise, they bind. With knowledge, they liberate.

sk: यः सर्वज्ञः सर्ववित्सर्वलक्ष्मीमयो हि सः तस्मादेतद्ब्रह्म नाम रूपं अन्नं च जायते तदेतत्सत्यम् ||
ro: yaḥ · sarva-jñaḥ · sarva-vit · sarva-lakṣmī-mayaḥ · hi · saḥ · tasmāt · etat · brahma · nāma · rūpaṁ · annaṁ · ca · jāyate · tat · etat · satyam ||
hi: जो सर्वज्ञ (omniscient) है, सर्ववित् (all-knowing) है, सर्वलक्ष्मीमय (endowed with all glory / सब ऐश्वर्य से युक्त) ही (indeed) वह (saḥ) है — उससे (तस्मात्) यह ब्रह्म (Vedic reality), नाम (name), रूप (form), और अन्न (food/matter) जायते (is born)। वह यह सत्यम् (truth / सत्य) है।
en: He who is omniscient (sarva-jña), all-knowing (sarva-vit), endowed with all glory (sarva-lakṣmī-maya) — He indeed is that [Brahman]. From Him are born this Brahman (the Vedic reality), name (nāma), form (rūpa), and food (anna). This is the truth (tat etat satyam).

ws.h: सब ऐश्वर्य / लक्ष्मी / glory से युक्त
ws.e: endowed with all glory — sarva (all) + lakṣmī (splendour/glory/prosperity/divine beauty) + maya (consisting of); Brahman possesses all splendour and excellence; not merely knowing but also beautiful, glorious, abundant
this is the truth — tat (that) + etat (this) + satyam (truth); a solemn closing formula affirming the truth of everything taught; used to seal the teaching with authority

gr: The closing seal of Khanda 2: this final mantra echoes and completes mantra 7, sealing the section with the solemn declaration 'tat etat satyam' — 'this is the truth.' The repetition from mantra 7: 'yaḥ sarva-jñaḥ sarva-vit' (He who is omniscient, all-knowing) — the phrase is repeated almost verbatim, creating a frame around the intervening mantras (8-10). This is a common Upanishadic structuring device — the same phrase opens and closes a section, enclosing the teachings within a frame of authority. sarva-lakṣmī-mayaḥ — 'endowed with all glory': this is a new attribute not in mantra 7. It adds to omniscience (sarva-jña) and omniscience of detail (sarva-vit) a third quality: all-splendour (sarva-lakṣmī). Brahman is not merely knowing but also glorious, beautiful, abundant. Lakṣmī here is not the goddess but the quality of divine splendour — all beauty, all prosperity, all excellence belongs to Brahman. tat etat satyam — 'this is the truth': the section closes with a formula of authentication — everything taught in this khanda (the bow-and-arrow meditation, OM, the heart-centre, the impossibility of liberation without God-knowledge, the creation through tapas) is declared to be satyam — truth. Not theory, not speculation, not opinion — truth.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_2.2.11 — This closing mantra echoes 1.1.9 and 2.2.7, creating structural unity across the Muṇḍaka. The addition of 'sarva-lakṣmī-mayaḥ' (endowed with all glory) is significant — it attributes aesthetic and material perfection to Brahman alongside intellectual omniscience. Ramanuja particularly emphasises this attribute as evidence of Brahman's saguṇa (qualified) nature — a Brahman that is 'all-glorious' cannot be nirguṇa (attribute-less). For Shankara, lakṣmī here refers to the śakti (power) aspect of Brahman in its saguṇa mode (Īśvara), not to nirguṇa Brahman itself. The closing formula 'tat etat satyam' is a solemn certification — the teacher stamps the entire teaching as truth. This formula appears in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (2.1.20, 5.4.1) and Chāndogya (3.14.4) as well.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'सर्वलक्ष्मीमयः' = सगुण ब्रह्म (qualified Brahman / Īśvara) — ऐश्वर्यवान्, शक्तिमान्। सगुण ब्रह्म से नाम-रूप-अन्न उत्पन्न। किन्तु निर्गुण ब्रह्म = सगुण से भी परे — गुण-रहित (attribute-less)। 'सत्यम्' = यह उपदेश = परम सत्य।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'sarva-lakṣmī-mayaḥ' = saguṇa Brahman (Īśvara) — endowed with splendour and power. From saguṇa Brahman, name-form-food are born. But nirguṇa Brahman = beyond even saguṇa — attribute-less. 'Satyam' = this teaching = the supreme truth.
advaita.ins: The glorious, all-knowing, all-splendid One — that's Brahman as creator, as the source of names, forms, and matter. Behind even that glory is the formless, the attribute-less. But this teaching is true — from the manifest glory to the formless source. All of it. Satyam.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'सर्वलक्ष्मीमयः' = भगवान् = सर्वगुण-सम्पन्न (endowed with all auspicious qualities) — ज्ञान, शक्ति, ऐश्वर्य, वीर्य, तेज, श्री — षड्गुण (six divine attributes)। यही सगुण ब्रह्म = परम सत्य — 'तदेतत्सत्यम्'।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'sarva-lakṣmī-mayaḥ' = the Lord = endowed with all auspicious qualities — knowledge, power, lordship, might, splendour, and grace — the six divine attributes. This saguṇa Brahman = the supreme truth — 'tat etat satyam.'
vishisht.ins: God is not just all-knowing — He is all-glorious. Every beauty, every excellence, every splendour in the universe is His. From that infinite glory, all creation flows — names, forms, matter. This is the truth. Not a theory. The truth.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'सर्वलक्ष्मीमयः' = चेतना = केवल ज्ञान (knowledge) नहीं — आनन्द (bliss), सौन्दर्य (beauty), ऐश्वर्य (splendour) भी। सच्चिदानन्द = सत् (being) + चित् (consciousness) + आनन्द (bliss) — तीनों अविभाज्य (inseparable)। 'सत्यम्' = यह अन्तिम सत्य = 'all is consciousness, all is bliss.'
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'sarva-lakṣmī-mayaḥ' = consciousness is not only knowledge — it is also bliss, beauty, and splendour. Sat-Chit-Ānanda = being + consciousness + bliss — all three inseparable. 'Satyam' = this is the final truth = 'all is consciousness, all is bliss.'
aurobindo.ins: The Divine isn't just the knower — it's the glory. All beauty, all splendour, all abundance is a face of consciousness. From that all-glorious consciousness, everything is born — names, forms, matter. This is the truth. Not a fragment of truth. The whole truth.

dp.q: 🔍 'Sarva-lakṣmī-maya' — Brahman as all-glorious
dp.a: The attribute 'sarva-lakṣmī-mayaḥ' ('endowed with all glory/splendour') adds an important dimension to the description of Brahman: What is lakṣmī here? Not the goddess Lakṣmī specifically, but the quality of lakṣmī — splendour, glory, beauty, prosperity, excellence. 'Sarva-lakṣmī-maya' means Brahman possesses ALL forms of excellence — every beauty, every splendour, every perfection in the universe. Why this matters: the Muṇḍaka has described Brahman as: (1) Omniscient (sarva-jña — knowing all in general). (2) All-knowing (sarva-vit — knowing every detail). (3) Now: All-glorious (sarva-lakṣmī-maya — possessing all beauty and excellence). This means Brahman is not merely a cosmic intelligence — cold, abstract, impersonal. Brahman is also beautiful, magnificent, glorious. The aesthetic dimension of reality is as divine as the intellectual dimension. The debate between schools: (1) Advaita: 'sarva-lakṣmī-maya' describes saguṇa Brahman (Īśvara) — Brahman in its creative, qualified aspect. Nirguṇa Brahman is beyond even glory. (2) Viśiṣṭādvaita: 'sarva-lakṣmī-maya' describes the REAL Brahman — Brahman IS all-glorious, and this glory is not a 'lower' aspect but Brahman's true nature. A Brahman without glory would be impoverished, not supreme. (3) Sri Aurobindo: 'sarva-lakṣmī-maya' = consciousness is inherently blissful and beautiful. Ānanda (bliss) and beauty are as fundamental as being (sat) and knowing (cit).

dp.q: 🔍 'Tat etat satyam' — the seal of truth
dp.a: The closing formula 'tat etat satyam' ('this is the truth') seals the entire Khanda 2 with a declaration of authentication: What 'satyam' means here: satyam is not merely 'truth' as opposed to 'falsehood.' It is ontological truth — that which IS, that which is real, that which cannot be contradicted or negated. When the teacher says 'this is satyam,' they are saying: 'everything I have taught — the bow-and-arrow meditation, OM, the heart-centre, the impossibility of liberation without God-knowledge, the creation through knowledge-tapas — all of this IS. It is not speculation, not opinion, not theory. It is reality.' The function of the formula: this is a teacher's seal — the equivalent of a signature on a legal document. The teacher stakes their authority on the truth of the teaching. What has been sealed: the entire Khanda 2 — from the opening paradox (āviḥ + guhā-caram) through the bow-and-arrow meditation (praṇava = dhanuḥ, ātmā = śara, brahma = lakṣya) to the impossibility verse (rolling up space) and the creation-through-tapas sequence. All of this is declared satyam. The Muṇḍaka's structure: Khanda 1 taught the cosmic Person and creation; Khanda 2 taught the meditation and the means to reach that Person. Together, they form the second Muṇḍaka — the practical heart of the Upanishad. The third Muṇḍaka will teach the result: the two birds, the cutting of the knot, and the final declaration 'brahma-vid brahmaiva bhavati.'
